#9690. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

Market Basket shows why strong results do not put a CEO beyond oversight, and why lawful board authority is not the same thing as business wisdom.

Strong operating results did not settle Market Basket's boardroom fight. On April 20, 2026, Vice Chancellor J. Travis Laster of the Delaware Court of Chancery upheld the suspension and subsequent firing of longtime president and CEO Arthur T. Demoulas, while acknowledging the company's operating success (DSM HoldCo). The central question was whether the directors acted in good faith in exercising their authority, not whether firing Demoulas was the best business choice.

The ruling separates authority to remove a CEO from the wisdom of that decision. This article and this series draw a broader governance lesson from that distinction: a board's job is to protect the company's enduring character and accountability, not just referee its machinery. The three-day trial addressed the narrower question of whether these directors acted lawfully (Moran; DSM HoldCo).

What Does the Business Judgment Rule Actually Protect?

The business judgment rule limits judicial second-guessing when it applies. In this case, Demoulas had to prove that a majority of the directors acted in bad faith. The court found that he failed to do so (DSM HoldCo). Laster took the case under submission on February 25, 2026, and issued his opinion on April 20. The outcome established that Demoulas had not met that burden, rather than that the board had chosen wisely. Honesty alone does not capture the rule's full requirements.

Market Basket's public story centers on low prices and loyal cashiers. In 2014, workers shut down stores for weeks to demand Demoulas's reinstatement after an earlier ouster by his cousins. The walkout made the chain a folk-hero story and ended in a $1.6 billion buyout that put Demoulas and his three sisters in sole control of the company (Chesto). Eleven years later, the boardroom fight pitted him against the sisters who had once helped bring him back. That history explains the public stakes; customer loyalty alone did not resolve the legal question.

Demoulas grew Market Basket into an operation generating roughly $8 billion in annual revenue and employing more than 30,000 people (Chesto). By any ordinary measure, he did his job well, and the court did not dispute that. Laster wrote that Demoulas "proved to be an excellent operator, but an imperious leader," adding that strong performance is "not the only dimension of a CEO's job" (DSM HoldCo).

The board's concerns extended beyond operating results. In August 2024, it gave Demoulas a five-item "Issues List" covering budgets, capital expenditure approvals, and succession, including rejecting automatic succession by his children. The opinion describes his failure to resolve those issues (DSM HoldCo). Reports of a possible walkout and boycott heightened the directors' concerns in spring 2025. They suspended him in May pending an outside investigation by Quinn Emanuel, then terminated him in September after unsuccessful mediation (DSM HoldCo; Solis). The investigation's conclusions supported the board's position. Those investigative conclusions and the court's findings represent separate parts of the record.

Two companies, DSM HoldCo and Demoulas Super Markets, brought the Section 225 action with directors Jay Hachigian, Steven Collins, and Michael Keyes to confirm the validity of Demoulas's removal. Demoulas counterclaimed that the directors breached their fiduciary duties by suspending and terminating him. He sought reinstatement as president and CEO (DSM HoldCo; Pelletiere and Boston 25 News Staff). At trial, he had to prove that a majority of the directors had acted in bad faith. He did not meet that burden. Laster rejected the claim that the directors were beholden to the sisters and found a rational basis for their concern about a repeat of 2014. The court upheld the removal (DSM HoldCo).

This case turns on a distinction between operating performance and governance cooperation, rather than a single verdict on a CEO. The two dimensions ask different questions. Collapsing them into one obscures what the court decided.

Operating performance covers revenue, growth, and customer loyalty, familiar subjects in shareholder letters. Governance cooperation asks different questions: whether management gives directors transparent information, plans succession honestly, and accepts that a board's authority to ask questions does not shrink as the business grows. Strong results and legitimate oversight address distinct responsibilities; neither cancels the other. The board, in turn, must exercise its authority for the company, not merely demand obedience.

Could the directors act independently of a powerful executive and obtain the information they needed to govern? Those are the two questions in the series' Independence and Information framework. In this dispute, their documentation began with unresolved issues in 2024 and continued through the May 2025 suspension pending investigation, the investigation itself, and unsuccessful mediation before termination. The court upheld their exercise of judgment on that record (DSM HoldCo). The documents supported the decision as evidence; the obligation to act in the company's interests remained.

The independence question starts with the family dispute. Outside status alone cannot establish a director's independence. Selection by one side of the family, by contrast, does not by itself prove bad faith. What matters is whether the directors exercised judgment for the company rather than serving a faction. The court rejected Demoulas's challenge on the record before it (DSM HoldCo).

None of this settles what Market Basket's culture or legacy required. Demoulas led a business with substantial employee and customer loyalty, and his supporters argue that the hands-on style they associate with "Artie T." helped sustain that success across roughly ninety stores. A spokesperson for Demoulas acknowledged that Delaware's deference to directors imposed high hurdles, but pointed to strong performance as evidence the company did not need fixing (Pelletiere and Boston 25 News Staff). That argument deserves a hearing. It is not a frivolous one.

The strongest objection concerns what removal would mean for the business. The directors could have authority to act without proving that firing Demoulas would preserve Market Basket's advantages better than a workable compromise. Strong results, meanwhile, could not put the CEO beyond oversight. The ruling resolves the legal challenge. It cannot show how the company would have fared under a different arrangement.

The unresolved business question leaves responsibilities intact on both sides. Strong operating results do not erase a board's oversight role. The board must exercise authority over management for the company, rather than treat control as an end in itself. Successful operations and legitimate oversight must coexist.

Section 225 supplied a focused procedure for determining whether Demoulas's removal was valid. The case moved from the September 2025 filing to the April 20, 2026 post-trial opinion in about seven months (DSM HoldCo; Vinson & Elkins). That pace gave this particular leadership dispute a prompt answer. The record also extended beyond the termination meeting: unresolved governance requests, an outside investigation, and unsuccessful mediation preceded the firing.

Ten days after the ruling, Market Basket named a former teenage bagger as its new president. Chuck Casassa, the operations director, joined the chain at fourteen in 1976. The April 30, 2026 announcement also marked the retirement of interim CEO Don Mulligan after more than four decades with the company, including 27 years as CFO (Riley). Separately, the board said the company was not for sale, would remain family-owned, and expected to work productively with Demoulas as a shareholder (Pelletiere and Boston 25 News Staff). Those statements describe the board's intentions. The long-term effects of its decision remain an open question.

The ruling gives family-company executives a clear answer to a recurring governance question: strong operating results do not put management beyond legitimate oversight. Performance is part of the job, not the whole job. Accountability matters too. Directors have a corresponding responsibility to exercise their authority on behalf of the company.

Nesgos, Nicholas J., Benjamin M. Greene, and Taylor Listau. "No Advance Notice Required: Delaware Chancery Upholds Board's Right to Remove CEO." ArentFox Schiff, 27 May 2026, www.afslaw.com/perspectives/alerts/no-advance-notice-required-delaware-chancery-upholds-boards-right-remove-ceo.

Chesto, Jon. "Judge Rules Against Arthur T. Demoulas in Market Basket Battle." The Boston Globe, 20 Apr. 2026, www.bostonglobe.com/2026/04/20/business/arthur-demoulas-market-basket-judge-ruling/.

#9688. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

The location detail is what separates this from ordinary proxy noise: AS2650 is a fixed, well-known allocation, so any exit node registered there is either a misconfiguration worth escalating internally or an actual beacon worth watching – there’s no third reading. That Infatica nodes bundled into free apps are the vector fits the broader pattern where the resource being rented out belongs to someone who never knowingly agreed to rent it. The persistent two-week window suggests nobody at the network’s edge was watching egress, which is the cheap fix here.

#9687. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

#9685. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9684. Claude Fable 5.2: Why Anthropic's Most Expensive Model Can End Up the Cheapest

Successful 18 years career track in IT and EdTech. Solid experience and knowledge of all business areas

Successful 18 years career track in IT and EdTech. Solid experience and knowledge of all business areas

Successful 18 years career track in IT and EdTech. Solid experience and knowledge of all business areas

Claude Fable 5.2 looks like a point release. It isn't. Here's what I think the model actually is, based on running Fable on real work: a different class of system that holds long tasks and keeps checking its own work; a model where the mode matters as much as the model itself; a model whose Max mode can do worse than Medium while costing five times more; and proof that you have to compare final results, not tokens.

My wife and I recently drove up to Napa, a wine region just north of San Francisco. On the way, I was talking with a friend, an entrepreneur. As always, the conversation turned to artificial intelligence and to the fact that I host ToTheMoon, an AI podcast from Silicon Valley. And, as always, we ran into the same thing. He said: "I use AI. We have different agents, we analyze our customers, our service runs on it."

I told him I'd give him the best advice of his life, at least when it comes to AI. Watch two ToTheMoon episodes where I break down the biggest AI trends, then rate yourself from 0 to 100 on how well you understand artificial intelligence. Right now you feel like a 60. Unless you're a deeply involved professional user, afterward you should feel like a zero.

By the way, when he said I understand AI pretty well, I told him I understand it at zero. Let me use Fable 5.2 to explain what I mean.

In November, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2. It seems like a small update: 5.1 became 5.2. What's the difference? Next to it sits Opus 5.5, OpenAI has its own lineups, and you can get lost in all of it.

Even Anthropic's own prompting guide notes that, in its testing, Fable 5.2 at its lowest effort level scored close to what Fable 5.1 did at higher levels. But the main thing is that Fable is a system of a different class — a different class of work altogether. To understand it, you have to start with where it came from.

Anthropic has a model family called Mythos. It's not available to regular people: only to special companies and specially approved individuals. These models were originally built for security — cybersecurity and finding vulnerabilities. One of the best-known cases came in late spring: these models were used to analyze a large number of open-source systems and found more than 10,000 different bugs and errors.

But such a model can not only find vulnerabilities — it can create them too. That's why Mythos models are probably the most advanced weapon in the world today when it comes to cybercrime and software.

Fable is the part of that family that's available to people. Ask it to analyze your own software — a website, a homegrown CRM, a server at home — and find vulnerabilities, and it will surface a fairly large number of serious problems. It lets you close holes that human programmers could never close — not this quickly, not this far in advance, and not at this scale. I may get a pile of comments from programmers for this. But I'm a former programmer myself, I know a fair amount about building systems, and I don't believe a human was ever capable of that.

Over the summer, Fable made an incredible splash — and became the first model the US government officially blocked, after reports that it could supposedly be used to build various kinds of weapons, both cyberweapons and offline ones. In general, models at the Mythos level make it possible to create serious biological weapons too — and, at the same time, to make very serious discoveries in medicine. There are several versions of why Anthropic clashed with the US authorities, from politics to marketing, and I went through them in the full episode. The outcome: the model was unblocked and released again after several changes. Alongside Fable 5.2, Anthropic also released Mythos 5.2, still for verified organizations only.

Remember the arc: released, blocked, reopened — but with restrictions and limits. We'll come back to it.

I first tried Fable before the block. I was in Santa Barbara, my kids were swimming in the pool, and I launched Claude Code from my phone.

I was blown away by the quality of its work. For the first time, a system worked this seriously — not small stuff, but big, serious tasks. You just described the task by voice, and it knew your infrastructure, understood what you wanted, and carried the task through to the end. It held a long working cycle, which, as we know, matters a lot in development: keeping the context going, forward and deep.

Modern models don't work only within your single context. While it works on the main task, Fable 5.2 keeps double-checking itself and launching new sessions in parallel. You don't have just one session running — parallel sessions start up, and something is always moving.

Double-checking is one of the ideas I keep repeating from episode to episode: on every important answer, I tell the system, "check yourself." Now a strong model does it on its own as well. Anthropic's guide says that at its highest effort levels in agentic coding, Fable 5.2 used subagents to review its own work — something Fable 5.1 didn't do on the same tasks.

And in the future, the task will already be done, while the session keeps working. That's the essence. This technology is essentially already in Dots in ChatGPT — Dots, by the way, is incredible. A friend and I rented a house up north for five days to lock ourselves in and work. As soon as the Airbnb booking email hit my inbox, Dots messaged me five minutes later: "I want to point out that you have conflicts. Your daughter has a concert on Sunday, and a piano tuner is coming to your place on Monday." I never asked it to do that.

Imagine the same for your own affairs. You signed a contract, agreed to hold an event, got everything ready — and a week later the law changed. And the system tells you: "Just a reminder: the rules have changed, the price has changed." It's great when a system can keep working after you've finished a task. For now, Dots doesn't spend huge compute on this, so the monitoring is still relative.

Ask your family which version of ChatGPT they use. My wife has used it for three years and is one of its 50 million active users. Which model, which number? She doesn't know. Does she understand the modes? Unlikely. She has a $20 paid plan with Medium selected. I usually tease everyone who doesn't pick a version and tell them: "Turn it up."

But that's normal. You don't know how many megapixels your iPhone has either. What normal person would know that? Except that this has created insane confusion in the market, and it persists: Low, Medium, High, Extra High, Max, Ultra — and the modes differ from product to product.

Once again: there's the model, and there's the mode. To compare Fable and Opus and figure out which is better, you need to understand what task you're doing and which mode you're working in.

And here's the catch. On a simpler model or a lower mode, a task can take three hours — and end up only 30% solved, or not solved at all. Another mode can solve it in ten minutes, 100%. In the end, on a more powerful model whose tokens cost much more and burn faster, you can spend less actual money.

Now the part that breaks people's brains. Fable's Max mode, I believe, costs three and a half times as much as Medium. And Max can do the task worse — while spending five times more money.

You might wonder: how can better reasoning be worse? That's the whole point: it can launch unnecessary agents, go in the wrong direction, and start doing things you don't need right now. It's a known fact that Fable models can lose context, stop abruptly, wander off, and launch extra agents.

Interestingly, Anthropic's own overview of Fable 5.2 says that most of the capability gain is already present at High, gains above it are uneven, and Max is for measuring the model's ceiling and for the rare task where time and tokens don't matter. At lower levels, the model is more likely to stop before the work is done; at higher ones, it delegates to subagents more readily.

For contrast, here's my most expensive story. I think it was July, right when OpenAI released Sol. I gave ChatGPT a task and walked away, and it worked on it for two and a half days. When I came back, I said: "So, did you solve it? I think you're stuck." And it replied: "I'm still working on the first item." It simply burned about 10 billion of my tokens. Fable, by the way, has never spent anything close to that for me.

Still, my advice is this. If you're not running out of tokens, use the maximum modes: in most cases, the maximum mode will give you a better result. But it's important to remember that it can do worse — many experiments won't show you that.

Take the cases people share around the world — say, a system cloning a Shopify-level site. One model in one mode spent $300, another spent $900 on the same thing, or the other way around. And if you compare all these cases with each other, you won't see any correlation about what's cheaper or what's right.

If you're watching a blogger who lays out ultimate rules — which mode and which model to pick, how tokens get spent, claiming he has tested everything — that's a conditional truth. Even for him, the same task can play out differently today and the day after tomorrow: models change, you don't know which test group you landed in, which country you were in, what account you had — and whether you got lucky.

Even official benchmarks don't give a simple answer. In September, Opus 5.5 came out: on terminal-based tests — maybe not a super-important metric — it scored 66%, while Fable had 55%. And I had a big question. If Fable is a system capable of hacking anything, with a colossal level of data analysis and system building, then what is this Opus 5.5, released to everyone, that outperforms it? Or did they make Fable worse? Many people remember that Fable got worse in July. Then, about six weeks later, Fable 5.2 came out — and it wins at complex programming by a lot. And complex programming is essentially any automation. It wins by multiples.

Price per token is only half the equation, too. According to Anthropic's price list, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens — 20% cheaper than Fable 5.1 and twice the price of Opus 5.5. But at one point on my $200 plan, Fable started eating all my tokens in four or five hours, and Fable 5.1 once ate my entire subscription allowance in two.

How can you even compare systems by tokens, when what you need to compare is the final result? You ask yourself: was the result achieved or not? And to figure out what works better, you have to run hundreds of different tasks, even the strangest ones.

If a task is routine, more or less small, or several different answers would work for you, you probably don't need Fable. In my view, Opus 5.5 is number one today for high-volume development, building business processes, and large-scale automation. At the same time, I remain a daily ChatGPT user — for chats and basic life tasks — and a Codex user. If you can afford two $100 plans, get ChatGPT for $100 and Anthropic for $100 — you'll feel a really strong effect.

Fable is like plugging a unique brain into a task. If you need the most thoroughly verified result with the highest final efficiency, Fable is very interesting:

A recent example. The other day I had one fairly complex task, and Opus 5.5 was working on it. Late at night, I switched it to Fable 5.2, because I didn't fully trust Opus. There was too much money riding on it.

An honest caveat. In my opinion, Fable definitely can't fully manage advertising on its own yet. But ad analysis — absolutely. And right now is a unique time, when you can squeeze a thousand times better ad setup out of Fable. Five years ago, no system existed that could squeeze out that kind of efficiency. A time will come when this is impossible to do — I guarantee it.

If you can't pay $200 every month, you can buy the $200 plan once and try to get something done with it. For organizing your finances, I specifically recommend Fable. It's worth at least understanding that a model this powerful exists.

That's the arc I mentioned: Fable was released, blocked, reopened — and then restrictions and limits came in. Most people, using free systems or a cheap subscription, don't even come close to having access to serious models. And to do the kind of things we're doing now, over time you'll have to pay tens of thousands of dollars. That's how it should be.

More than a year ago, Sam Altman described a very interesting case, and I think it's very viable. He said a time will come when you tell yourself, "I have $20,000 to solve this problem," hand it to AI, and it solves it. We're not there yet, because right now you pay after the fact: you can spend $20,000 and it won't even start the task, or it'll go the wrong way. Today, AI can't really plan its own spending.

But the logic itself is right. People come to me very often about starting a business. I tell them: "You shouldn't start a business. You can pay me $10,000 — I just gave you good advice, because you'll save a hundred." People aren't used to paying like that, but it's the right price. If you're putting $100,000–$200,000 into a business, and your chance of losing is about 80% from the start — and it usually is — then paying AI $5,000 to work through your problem is the right move.

People don't do this because they think in terms of expenses. They'd rather spend that $5,000 on a vacation, a hotel, a bag, or a couch than invest it in the right financial strategy for their household, a financial strategy for their business, or a marketing management system.

I often run into this exchange. "Who runs your ads?" "We do it ourselves." "But you don't know advertising." "Well, we can't hire anyone right now; our whole ad budget is $1,500." Then at least pay $300 for ad analysis by these AI systems and spend $1,200 on the ads. Actually, you don't even need to pay the $300: it's about 10% of a $200 plan.

I believe every ordinary person should now build business processes. Even my wife. Because in the near future, it will be less and less clear whom you can trust with a given task.

Right now you can still buy something without being manipulated and see something without being manipulated. But we're moving into a time when manipulation becomes far more serious than it is now. My kids are already growing up in an era of super-manipulation: there are incredibly many channels for influencing a person. And we're entering an era when artificial intelligence will truly know who you are. Everything before that was kindergarten.

I started saying this about fifteen years ago: I deeply disliked the market of deception in professional marketing. Marketers all said, "We know our customers, we've studied them, we've analyzed them." But that doesn't compare to what it means to know your customer the way artificial intelligence does now.

Back to the drive from Napa. I asked my friend what he uses. "I have a ChatGPT subscription, I use DeepSeek." And I think he said he has Claude Code. I asked, "How much is your most expensive subscription?" "Twenty dollars." That's it — zero, right away. And he's a businessman with millions of dollars in monthly revenue. Then I heard DeepSeek, and I immediately got bored.

How do you even measure how well someone understands AI? A surgeon has parameters: how many operations, how many hours of surgery, the longest operation, where they studied, whom they worked with. A pilot has flight hours, countries flown, tough situations, aircraft types. But assessing how well a person grasps AI for their life is very hard today.

Even the people who create AI — Sam Altman, Dario Amodei — understand it very strategically, as visionaries. But many of them would find it hard to grasp the newest use cases — unless they're fanatics who build systems and create use cases themselves every day. Judging by their interviews, most of them aren't fanatics of these systems. Yet we're used to trusting: if someone talks about AI and has a hundred billion dollars, everyone assumes they understand it. And having worked as a programmer for forty years doesn't mean you understand AI. I recently read a programmer with twenty years of experience writing that he doesn't want to and won't use AI because it harms the tech world.

So your task today is to figure out what level of development and perception of AI you're at, and to keep checking against it. If you care about your professional growth, your business, your education, and your future, honestly rate yourself from 0 to 100. The gap between those who truly use AI and everyone else is already cosmic. And it will be catastrophic — and you won't even notice when it happens.

Tell me in the comments what level you see in yourself. Do you know which model you're using and why you chose it? Have you tried Fable 5.2 or Opus 5.5?

Alexander Volchek is an entrepreneur and builder, a strategic advisor to 200+ startups and scale-ups, and the host of ToTheMoon, an independent AI media outlet from Silicon Valley. Episodes, breakdowns, and company dossiers: besolid.com/tothemoon. YouTube: @ToTheMoonTech.

#9682. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.
