#9662. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. #9660. When Your Crypto Turns Red: How to Respond to a Market Crash

You go into crypto expecting a return, preferably a steady one that doesn't take forever to arrive. Then prices fall, and the investment you hoped would reward you starts losing value instead. It's an uncomfortable part of investing, but it needn't become a personal crisis: anyone intending to stick around for years has to learn to cope with losses as well as enjoy the gains.

Experience and a carefully drawn plan don't guarantee a profit. In a market prone to abrupt price swings, with the fear and greed index reflecting changing sentiment, setbacks deserve a place in your thinking. A guide on how to buy XRP explains the practical steps of getting started, but learning how to handle a position that's losing value usually involves experience of your own.

Fortunately, you can do some preparation before a crash arrives. If you know which parts of the situation to examine and what decisions you'll need to make, you have a better chance of working through the difficulty with a clear idea of what you're doing. The following steps are a place to start.

Managing the feelings around an investment comes before managing the investment itself. Crypto's hectic price movements make that a demanding exercise, particularly in a downturn, when mounting pressure makes an impulsive response seem attractive. Keeping a clear head at that point takes effort; knowing in advance that you'll be tested helps you recognize what's happening.

A loss on screen isn't an instruction to panic. Whether you're thinking of selling or treating the fall as a chance to add to your holdings, the decision needs reasons you can examine. Otherwise, the fear pushing you out of a position and the excitement drawing you further in can both take over the process. How do you give reason a chance to catch up?

Start by stopping for a moment. That pause is a small achievement because it interrupts the rush to do something immediately, when the pressure can make it difficult to see beyond the next click. Once you've made room to think, use it to consider the situation before committing yourself.

If you've already worked out a strategy and know what you want from the investment, bring those goals back into view. Would the sale you're considering, or the extra purchase, actually help you get there? Spending a little time on that question can settle some of the uncertainty, because you're looking at the decision in relation to a purpose you chose before the pressure built up.

Once you've got a grip on your emotions, look at the downturn over a longer stretch of time. The damage to your investments can be frightening, and you may feel like getting out altogether. But consider how many declines crypto has already been through: rising and falling markets are recurring phases in its history, although some falls have lasted much longer and cut much deeper than others.

Volatility has been part of crypto for as long as investors have been putting money into it, so learning to live with rising and falling prices is one of the first lessons. The rollercoaster comparison fits for a reason. You can be enjoying a climb only to find yourself heading down again, with little certainty about where the next twist will take you.

Being in the red today doesn't tell you that recovery is out of the question. The wider crypto market has recovered from earlier falls, so its cycles offer some perspective when pessimism starts taking over. Keep the distinction clear, though: that history doesn't mean every project survives or that every coin returns to its old price.

One decline may look much like another on a chart while differing in what caused it, how severe it is and how long it lasts. Trouble inside crypto can be the trigger, from a failed project to the collapse of an exchange. Mt. Gox's bankruptcy in February 2014 is one such example: confidence in exchanges suffered, and the shock added pressure to prices across the market.

The pressure can come from wider economic events, too. In November 2021, the Federal Reserve chose to slow its asset purchases, so it was still adding to its holdings, but at a reduced pace. That's a change in monetary support, not the same thing as an exchange collapsing. Find out which influences have contributed to the decline in your coins: understanding the reason for the fall helps you judge what may follow and decide how to act.

Getting a crypto forecast right is difficult, and plenty turn out to be wrong. You can still read them for the different ways events might unfold, using the possible market directions to think through your options without treating any one scenario as settled.

Crypto's longer-term future isn't something you can pin down, but working through those scenarios should leave you better prepared to choose a course of action. If you think the lower price creates an opportunity, you could keep your coins or buy more to build the holding. If your assessment points to a more severe and prolonged fall, selling a weak asset may be the response you choose instead, accepting the loss if the sale is below what you paid. By then, you should be choosing a response to the situation, rather than making a trade just to silence the worry.

When you can't make sense of the outlook, you can choose to sell only part of the holding and keep the remainder in case prices recover. Whatever you decide, let your overall strategy and the amount of risk you can tolerate determine the choice.

#9659. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9658. A reader found a hole in our AI inbox. Postgres closes it now

Posted on Nov 17 • Edited on Nov 17 • AI-assisted

In my last post I wrote about how our AI assistant can write to exactly one table. Claude, connected to Reperline over MCP, can only insert rows into pending_changes. A person approves or rejects each one in an inbox, and apply_pending_change writes the real tables with the approver's own rights.

I ended that post with "the inbox is where the real control happens". In the comments, Mike Johnstone pointed out that the inbox had a hole of its own:

A proposal can go stale in the inbox too. If someone changes a milestone before approval, the reviewer may be looking at a diff against an old value.

He was right, and the bug was worse than a confusing screen. This post is the fix, migration 064.

A milestone proposal carries an absolute value, not a delta:

Progress just went down by five points. Our normal entry path refuses to lower progress without a note explaining why, but that rule lived in the application function that records a fact from the UI and Telegram. The approval path wrote the journal directly, so the drop went in silently. Nobody did anything wrong, and the database accepted a value that was already false when it was approved.

The grants from the first post did their job. Claude still wrote nothing by itself. A person approved a stale diff, and the approval was the hole.

The quick fix is to show the current value next to the proposal and hope the reviewer notices. We do show it now, but a check that lives only on the screen is the same kind of promise the first post was about avoiding. Another client, a script or a second tab can still approve. The check had to be inside apply_pending_change, in the same transaction as the write.

Mike suggested storing the base row version with the proposal. The idea is right; choosing which version took most of the work.

A row version such as xmin. It changes on any update of the milestone row, including a renamed milestone or a corrected planned date. Every unrelated edit would strand every open proposal.

The current progress value alone. It misses the case 70 → 55 → 70: someone records a drop, then measures again and records 70. The value is back where it was, but two facts were entered that the proposal never saw. The reviewer should look again.

The id or timestamp of the latest journal row. Facts can be back dated (reported_at is when the work was measured, not when it was typed), so "latest by reported_at" misses a late entry of an older measurement. created_at is the transaction start time, so rows inserted in one transaction tie, and a transaction that started earlier can commit later.

What we used: the number of journal rows plus the progress value. Every fact for a milestone is a new row in milestone_updates, and a trigger moves milestones.progress on every insert. So the count changes exactly when progress may have changed, regardless of dates. Comparing progress as well covers the remaining blind spot (a delete plus an insert keeps the count). Our app never deletes a fact, but the role technically still holds DELETE, so we did not want to rely on that.

If Claude sent the base, a prompt could make it send whatever value makes the check pass. So the base is stamped by a BEFORE INSERT trigger, and anything the client put in those keys is overwritten:

In apply_pending_change the milestone branch now does this before writing:

The split into two statements matters. Under READ COMMITTED, each statement inside a PL/pgSQL function gets a fresh snapshot. If the count ran in the same statement as the lock, it could use a snapshot taken before the lock was granted. A fact that committed while we were waiting would be missing from the count, and we would approve over it.

The lock also closes the window from the other side. Inserting a fact takes a KEY SHARE lock on the milestone (the foreign key) and the trigger then updates the row, so no fact can land between our check and our own journal insert.

is distinct from instead of <> matters too: it treats null as a value, so a null base never compares equal to anything.

Rejecting is never checked. A stale proposal can always be thrown away; it just cannot be approved.

The UI shows the same thing the database enforces. A stale proposal gets a red notice ("It was 55% when proposed. A fact was entered since, so the proposal can only be rejected.") and a disabled Approve button. That is a display hint only. The function refuses on its own, and the error key proposal_stale is translated for anyone who reaches it some other way.

Proposals that were already waiting when the migration ran were backfilled with the current state, so the existing inbox was not stranded by the upgrade.

Each case runs against a real Postgres, with Claude's role filing the proposal:

That last one is the case that is easiest to get wrong and hardest to see in review, so it is the one I would not ship without.

The first post was about making sure the AI cannot write. This one is about the next layer: a person approving is only meaningful if they approve against the data as it is now. Optimistic concurrency is an old idea; the work was in choosing a version marker that changes when it should and only then, and in making the stamp something the proposer cannot fake.

And thanks to Mike. A comment section that finds a real bug in a week is worth more than any launch post.

If you are building an approval inbox for an AI agent: store what the proposal was based on, stamp it on the server, and check it under a lock in the same transaction that writes.

#9656. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9654. Can We Build Human-Like AI Before We Understand the Human Condition?

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

The technology industry is racing to build artificial intelligence that can reason, communicate and increasingly behave in ways that seem human.

But there is an obvious paradox in that ambition: science still does not fully understand the extraordinary mind we are trying to reproduce.

In 2016, __an editorial in the academic journal *History of the Human Sciences *__presented the problem in stark terms: despite incredible advances in fields such as molecular biology, evolutionary psychology, artificial intelligence and cognitive neuroscience, one central category continued to resist definition: “the human.”

The importance of that problem had been expressed more directly decades earlier by psychologist B. F. Skinner, who wrote in his 1974 book About Behaviorism that that “the major problems facing the world today can be solved only if we improve our understanding of human behavior.”

That question has become even more relevant as AI systems have grown more capable. What exactly are the characteristics that distinguish human intelligence? How did consciousness emerge? And how did our remarkable cognitive abilities develop alongside insecurity, aggression, cooperation, creativity and psychological conflict?

These questions form part of the much older scientific and intellectual problem of understanding the human condition.

Nearly four centuries ago, philosopher and scientist René Descartes, while probing the nature of the thinking mind, described the intellectual predicament in striking terms:

“So serious are the doubts into which I have been thrown…that I can neither put them out of my mind nor see any way of resolving them. It feels as if I have fallen unexpectedly into a deep whirlpool…”.

Almost four centuries later, consciousness remains one of the most difficult pieces of the puzzle.

Philosopher David Chalmers, co-director of New York University’s Center for Mind, Brain and Consciousness, famously distinguished the relatively tractable problem of explaining cognitive functions with what he termed the “hard problem” of consciousness: explaining why information processing is accompanied by subjective experience.

But consciousness is not only a question of subjective experience. It also gave humans an extraordinary capacity to understand the relationship between events, anticipate outcomes and increasingly manage behaviour on the basis of that understanding.

There is also an evolutionary puzzle. If the ability to understand cause and effect and consciously adjust behaviour provides such an advantage, why did anything approaching full human consciousness emerge so rarely in evolutionary history?

These questions are approached from different directions by philosophy, neuroscience and evolutionary biology. Together they illustrate how much remains unresolved about the mind that AI increasingly seeks to emulate.

They also raise another question about the human condition: what psychological consequences followed when humans acquired this extraordinary capacity for conscious self-management?

Australian biologist Jeremy Griffith approaches the problem from an evolutionary direction. His explanation of the human condition asks what happened when a conscious, understanding-dependent intellect emerged within an organism already equipped with genetically acquired instincts.

Griffith places the emergence of consciousness, and this resulting conflict with instincts, at roughly two million years ago, linking it to the major development of the brain’s association cortex during human evolution.

Natural selection can provide a species with inherited instinctive orientations, while a conscious mind develops understanding by experimenting with cause and effect. Griffith proposes that as our distant hominin ancestors became sufficiently conscious to manage life through understanding, their experiments inevitably began departing from established instinctive orientations. The instincts inevitably resisted those departures, and that orientating ‘pressure’ amounted, in effect, to criticism of an emerging intellect that could not yet explain why its experiments were necessary.

Griffith argues that the insecurity that resulted from this seemingly unwarranted criticism produced defensive reactions of anger, egocentricity and alienation. His hypothesis therefore interprets these troubled characteristics primarily as psychological responses to the emergence of consciousness rather than simply manifestations of selfish or aggressive instinct-based instincts.

Stephen Hawking once observed that while physics and mathematics may tell us how the universe began, they are “not much use in predicting human behavior because there are far too many equations to solve.” It is precisely this seemingly impenetrable complexity that Griffith’s hypothesis accounts for, presenting a framework in which the full spectrum of human behaviour, including its many apparently contradictory aspects, can be made sense of. Its proponents argue that the more fully Griffith’s explanation is understood, the more persuasive it becomes, a view reflected in the growing number of favourable assessments it has received from scientists and academics who have examined his work.

This also gives the hypothesis a further implication. If the insecurity arose because the conscious intellect could not explain why it had to depart from instinct, Griffith argues that gaining that understanding would resolve the original conflict. On his account, anger, egocentricity and alienation are therefore not immutable features of human nature, but defensive responses that can become redundant once their underlying cause is understood.

To advance research, discussion and public understanding of the human condition Griffith established the international charity Fix The World.

Neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene, who’s based at the Collège de France, has approached consciousness from a very different direction. His global neuronal workspace model proposes that conscious access occurs when information becomes globally available across a distributed network of brain regions, allowing it to be shared with otherwise specialised cognitive systems.

Chalmers, Dehaene and Griffith are therefore asking different questions and proposing fundamentally different explanations. Chalmers focuses on why subjective experience exists, Griffith on the evolutionary and psychological consequences of consciousness emerging in humans, and Dehaene on the neural mechanisms associated with conscious access.

Together they illustrate a larger point: understanding consciousness remains a substantial scientific and philosophical frontier.

For AI developers, the immediate challenge is not necessarily to solve the human condition. Today’s systems can reproduce remarkable aspects of human language and reasoning without requiring science to possess a complete theory of human nature.

But the closer the ambition moves toward genuinely human-like intelligence, the more difficult the unanswered questions become to ignore.

What distinguishes intelligence from consciousness? How did human consciousness arise? Why are emotion, insecurity, morality, cooperation and conflict so deeply entangled with human cognition? And which of these characteristics, if any, would accompany a genuinely conscious artificial intelligence?

What there is instead is a continuing endeavour across neuroscience, evolutionary biology, psychology, philosophy and now artificial intelligence to understand the mind that makes us human.

#9652. Building an AI-Simulated Client for Counselling Training: Lessons From PraxisAI

An AI-simulated client is an AI-powered character that allows trainees to practise realistic counselling conversations without requiring a human role-play partner for every session. The system can respond to what the trainee says, maintain a scenario, adapt the conversation and provide structured feedback after the session.

That is the idea behind PraxisAI, an AI human-skills simulation and assessment platform built by ThinkShift. Trainee counsellors can practise conversations with AI clients through voice, avatar and chat, with sessions evaluated against defined competencies.

The interesting engineering challenge isn't simply making an AI that can talk.

It is making an AI that can stay inside a scenario, behave consistently, create a useful training experience and turn a conversation into measurable feedback.

That became the core problem we explored while building PraxisAI.

An AI-simulated client is a virtual client powered by AI for training or role-play.

Instead of following a fixed dialogue tree, the simulated client can respond dynamically to the trainee's questions and statements. This makes the interaction less predictable than traditional scripted practice.

For counselling training, that distinction matters.

A trainee shouldn't only practise asking a predefined list of questions. They need to experience what happens when a conversation changes direction, when a client gives an unexpected answer, or when important information emerges gradually.

Recent research has started evaluating generative AI in exactly this role. Studies have found that AI can provide a flexible environment for practising counselling skills, while also identifying limitations around emotional nuance, authenticity, cultural dynamics and overly agreeable responses.

How do you make an AI conversation useful for learning, rather than simply interesting to interact with?

Traditional role-play is valuable, but it has practical limitations.

Two students need to be available at the same time. One person has to play the client. The scenario may change depending on the person playing the role. And repeating the same exercise many times isn't always easy.

A trainee can practise a scenario, review the interaction, try again and compare the results.

Practice → Conversation → Feedback → Reflection → Practice again

The value is not that AI replaces a supervisor or a human client.

The value is that it can create additional opportunities to practise between structured teaching and real-world experience.

Research published in 2025 similarly found that AI-simulated counselling sessions could offer a psychologically safer and flexible environment for practice, while concluding that AI should supplement rather than replace live training.

A useful training simulator needs to do more.

Imagine a scenario where a client is initially reluctant to discuss a particular problem.

If the trainee asks an open-ended question, the client might gradually reveal more.

If the trainee interrupts or asks a leading question, the client might respond differently.

If the trainee demonstrates empathy and creates space, the conversation may develop in another direction.

The system therefore needs to maintain more than conversational fluency.

That means keeping track of things such as:

Without this context, an AI client can quickly start behaving like a generic assistant.

Realism doesn't mean making the AI sound human in every sentence.

In a training environment, realism means creating behaviour that makes sense within the scenario.

These behaviours create opportunities for the trainee to practise actual communication skills.

Research into AI-simulated counselling has identified a similar challenge: AI can produce convincing interactions, but overly idealised responses, limited emotional nuance and missing non-verbal cues can reduce authenticity.

That means realism has to be treated as a product design problem, not just an LLM prompt.

This was one of the biggest distinctions in building PraxisAI.

A training simulator has a learning objective.

For example, the objective might be to help a trainee practise reflective listening.

The system then needs to evaluate the conversation against that competency rather than simply deciding whether the final answer sounded good.

This creates a second layer around the AI conversation:

AI client → conversation → competency evaluation → feedback

That second layer is where the product becomes a training system.

A realistic conversation followed by useful feedback is much more useful.

After a practice session, trainees need to understand what happened.

Instead of receiving a generic score such as:

the feedback should connect the assessment to the actual interaction.

This creates a connection between what happened and what to practise next.

PraxisAI is designed around this assessment layer, with sessions evaluated against competencies rather than treating the conversation as an isolated chatbot interaction.

One of the interesting product challenges is that counselling isn't one single skill.

Different approaches can emphasise different techniques and competencies.

So an assessment system needs to understand the context in which a conversation is taking place.

That means the evaluation layer needs to consider:

Scenario + approach + conversation + competency framework

This is important because the same response could be appropriate in one context and less useful in another.

The assessment therefore becomes part of the product architecture, not something added after the AI conversation has been built.

Another useful distinction is between practice and assessment.

During practice, the trainee is learning.

They may want guidance, feedback and opportunities to repeat a scenario.

During assessment, the objective is different: the trainee should demonstrate their skills with less intervention.

Separating these experiences makes the product more useful because the system is supporting two different user goals.

This is a broader lesson for AI product development:

Don't build one AI experience and expect it to serve every stage of the user's journey.

The AI behaviour, interface and evaluation system should change according to what the user is trying to accomplish.

PraxisAI is designed around multiple interaction formats, including voice, avatar and chat.

This creates another product consideration.

Text-based interaction gives the system a clean representation of the conversation.

Voice introduces additional dimensions such as:

An avatar adds another visual layer to the experience.

The underlying training objective, however, should remain consistent.

The interface can change without losing the core learning loop:

Interact → Evaluate → Understand → Improve

That separation between the interaction layer and the learning layer is useful when designing AI training products.

It is easy to demonstrate an AI role-play by writing a detailed prompt.

Building a reliable product around that interaction is much harder.

You need scenario management, user flows, evaluation logic, feedback, persistence and a clear learning objective.

Giving an AI complete freedom doesn't necessarily produce the best simulation.

The AI should have enough freedom to create natural conversations while remaining consistent with the scenario and learning objective.

If every assessment is generated from scratch, results can become inconsistent.

A useful training system needs defined competencies and a consistent evaluation framework.

The AI can then interpret the conversation within those boundaries.

The most visible part of an AI simulator is the conversation.

But the less visible parts, scenario setup, evaluation, feedback and progress tracking, may create much of the product's actual value.

This is perhaps the most important lesson.

AI simulation can create more practice opportunities, but it doesn't reproduce everything that happens in a real human interaction.

Current research continues to identify limitations around emotional depth, authenticity, cultural sensitivity and non-verbal communication.

"Replace human counselling practice with AI."

"Use AI to make structured practice more accessible and repeatable."

PraxisAI is one example of the type of AI product development we work on at ThinkShift.

ThinkShift is based in Dubai and focuses on building working products that can be tested with real users rather than spending months building around assumptions.

That approach influenced how we thought about PraxisAI.

"How can we build a chatbot for counsellors?"

"What would make AI genuinely useful for someone learning counselling skills?"

That change in framing affected the product.

The AI conversation became one component.

And the feedback loop connected everything together.

That is an important distinction when building AI products in Dubai—or anywhere else.

The technology is only one part of the product. The real work is connecting the technology to a measurable user problem.

AI-simulated clients should be considered a supplement to human-led training, not a replacement for supervisors, educators or real human interaction.

Research from 2025 found promising results for AI-assisted counselling practice, including improvements in trainee confidence and reductions in anxiety in one study, but the researchers also emphasised the need for thoughtful integration and further research.

Human interaction still brings qualities that AI cannot perfectly reproduce:

AI can provide another layer of practice.

It shouldn't pretend to be the complete training environment.

An AI-simulated client is an AI-powered character designed to interact with a trainee in a practice scenario. It can respond dynamically to the trainee while maintaining the context and objectives of the scenario.

AI role-play training places a learner inside a simulated conversation with an AI character. The AI responds according to the scenario, while the learner practises specific skills. The interaction can then be reviewed and evaluated.

Yes. Recent research has evaluated generative AI as a simulated client for counselling role-play and found potential value as a supplementary training tool. However, researchers have also identified limitations involving realism, emotional nuance and cultural context.

An AI conversation simulator is a system that generates interactive conversations for training, practice or assessment. Unlike a fixed script, it can respond dynamically to what the user says.

The main benefits include repeatable practice, flexible access to scenarios, lower-pressure practice environments and structured feedback. It can give trainees additional opportunities to practise before working with real people.

An AI training system can analyse a conversation against predefined competencies and identify specific moments that demonstrate or miss those competencies. The feedback can then explain what happened and suggest areas for improvement.

It can create increasingly realistic scenarios, but realism depends on scenario design, context, prompting and evaluation. Current research still identifies limitations in emotional nuance, cultural responsiveness and non-verbal communication.

AI simulations can struggle with subtle emotions, cultural context, non-verbal signals and the unpredictability of genuine human interactions. They should therefore be used with appropriate educational guidance and human oversight.

No. AI can supplement role-play by providing additional practice opportunities, but it should not replace human supervision, education or real-world interpersonal experience.

Building an AI-simulated client taught us that the difficult part isn't making AI talk.

The difficult part is making the conversation useful.

For a training product, that means thinking beyond the model:

Scenario → Interaction → Competency → Assessment → Feedback → Improvement

Once those pieces work together, an AI conversation stops being just a demonstration of generative AI.

It becomes a tool for structured practice.

And that is the direction we are exploring with PraxisAI: using applied AI to help people practise important human skills more often, receive better feedback and become more prepared for real-world interactions.

#9651. Modus CTO Explains Why Static AI Skills Are Becoming a Bottleneck for Enterprise AI

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

AI agents may be processing hundreds of lines of instructions to complete tasks that require only a handful of details. According to Modus, median context-loading precision is below 1%, while even results at the 90th percentile remain below 10%. The finding highlights a growing challenge for enterprise AI: providing agents with relevant, up-to-date knowledge without overwhelming them with unnecessary information.

In a recent blog post, Tomer Mesika, Co-Founder and CTO of Modus, argues that static AI skills are contributing to this problem. While these instructions encode organizational workflows and technical knowledge, they also contain operational details that inevitably change. As companies deploy more agents, keeping these instructions accurate becomes increasingly difficult.

Mesika proposes moving toward dynamic skills, where information is assembled at runtime based on the task, the current state of the organization, and the user's permissions.

Static skills often combine two different things: instructions describing how work should be performed and operational facts needed to execute it. The first might include deployment procedures or incident response practices. The second includes database names, cloud account IDs, API endpoints, Slack channels, and feature flags.

The problem is that these facts change constantly. A database gets renamed, a team changes its communication channel, or an infrastructure resource is replaced. The skill remains unchanged unless someone remembers to update it.

Mesika compares this to using a printed map after the surrounding infrastructure has changed. The instructions may look reliable, but their underlying information is no longer accurate.

MCP addresses part of the challenge by allowing agents to retrieve live information from connected systems. However, freshness does not guarantee relevance. MCP is the communication mechanism; the missing piece is determining what information should travel through it for a particular task and user.

Mesika's proposed solution is to separate organizational processes from the facts required to execute them.

Instead of hard-coding an account ID or communication channel into a skill, organizations can use meaningful placeholders such as "Production AWS account ID" or "On-call channel." The underlying process remains stable, while the corresponding information is resolved when an agent needs it.

"Static skills are essentially caches without invalidation. They preserve a snapshot of what an agent needed to know when someone originally wrote them, even as the underlying organization changes," said Mesika. "The goal should be to keep the process durable while computing the facts an agent needs for each task, based on the latest available information and the user's permissions."

This approach allows agents to receive just-in-time skills containing only the operational details relevant to their immediate requests.

Making dynamic skills work requires more than rewriting instructions. Organizations need infrastructure capable of collecting, connecting, verifying, and continuously updating their operational knowledge.

Mesika outlines an approach that pulls information directly from authoritative sources, including cloud accounts, Slack, Git, databases, feature flags, and internal documentation. Rather than treating this information as disconnected text, the system maps entities and their relationships.

For example, an agent working on a payments service should be able to identify its production account, associated database, kill-switch flag, and on-call channel. Each fact also needs metadata covering its source, last verification, ownership, and access permissions.

This is the foundation of a Context Warehouse: a continuously maintained layer of enterprise knowledge that supplies AI systems with the information they need.

Modus is developing this architecture through its platform, using connectors to gather organizational context from existing enterprise tools. Its Context Warehouse organizes information into context items with source details, hierarchical relationships, and permissions inherited from the original systems.

When an agent connects through MCP, it communicates its intent rather than requesting a specific file. Modus selects and assembles the relevant information, filters it according to the user's permissions, and measures how much of the available context was actually needed.

Permissions are also checked with every read rather than relying on previously cached access information.

For enterprise leaders, the takeaway is that improving AI agents may require rethinking the infrastructure behind the instructions they receive. Building dynamic skills involves continuous synchronization, entity mapping, metadata management, and permission-aware retrieval. These capabilities go well beyond prompt engineering or creating more specialized instruction files.

As organizations move toward more autonomous AI systems, the challenge will be giving agents access to knowledge that reflects how the business operates today. Static skills can preserve how work should be done, but a Context Warehouse can provide what agents need to do it now.

#9649. Stop the agent from wrapping every handler in useMemo “for performance”

The PR “cleans up” a form by wrapping every event handler in useCallback and every derived boolean in useMemo. The commit message says “performance.” There is no profile, no skipped render that mattered, and two stale-closure bugs in the validation path.

I’ve started treating agent-added useMemo / useCallback without a stated reason as noise, not as an optimization. React is not cheaper just because the call site looks official. The wrappers are extra dependencies to get wrong.

The model has been trained on a lot of “always memoize callbacks passed to children” advice. Some of that advice was aimed at class components, or at a child wrapped in memo that actually sits in a hot list. A one-off

#9648. Inventory Moxa OnCell assets before treating CVE-2026-111461 as patched

A CVE record can create an assumption that a vendor patch exists somewhere and that the main task is deployment. CVE-2026-111461 breaks that assumption. The affected OnCell G3150A-LTE Series is end of life, and Moxa's mitigation is to keep SMS management disabled rather than to install a new firmware release for this line.

Moxa's MPSA-269510 advisory assigns CVE-2026-111461 to an OS command injection flaw in the OnCell G3150A-LTE Series. The issue is CWE-78, the CVSS 4.0 score is 7.5, and the SMS upgrade argument reaches system() without escaping. The vendor says all firmware versions are affected and unauthenticated remote exploitation does not apply.

The advisory also covers CVE-2026-111459 and CVE-2026-111460. An inventory should preserve the exact CVE and product relationship instead of treating the whole advisory as a generic Moxa event.

An operator cannot disable SMS on an unknown gateway. An operator also cannot verify a management path when a device is represented only by a spreadsheet row with no network owner. The first evidence gap is usually completeness.

Build a list from procurement records, network discovery, firewall addresses, and site maintenance logs. Match each candidate against the OnCell G3150A-LTE Series. Record firmware, site, operational purpose, management address, account owner, SMS state, and replacement status. Mark duplicate addresses and devices behind NAT so that a count is not mistaken for a unique asset count.

Configuration records age quickly. A device that was installed with SMS disabled may have been changed during a field test or restored from a backup that enabled it. Verify the setting on the device or through an approved management channel.

The same applies to privileges. The CVE requires high privileges, so the account list is part of the inventory. Determine which users can perform SMS or upgrade operations and whether shared or stale accounts remain.

ZoomEye returned 330 matches for app="Moxa OnCell". The exact CVE query returned 0. The product count is not proof of vulnerability, and the zero CVE result does not mean no affected assets exist. The comparison is useful because a product fingerprint can reveal a gateway that the internal inventory missed.

Do not place an external match directly into a victim list. Verify ownership, reachability, configuration, and evidence of compromise separately.

For each affected gateway, choose one of three documented states: retired, approved for controlled use with SMS disabled, or approved for controlled use with SMS enabled for a specific operational requirement. The last state needs a stronger exception with limited access, monitoring, and an end date.

Moxa's general recommendations support this approach. Limit communication to trusted networks, avoid direct internet exposure, disable unused services, enforce least privilege, and review logs. None of those controls should remain only in a policy document.

The inventory is ready for risk decisions when every known OnCell device has an owner and verified SMS state, management-network paths are documented, and every remains-in-service exception has an accountable approver. That is a higher bar than a scanner count, and a more useful one for an end-of-life command injection flaw.

#9647. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9644. Hybrid Search, Measured

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at trida.ai

Ask a retrieval system about one error code and it may answer from the record for a different one. The two records read almost identically: same service, same shape of incident, codes differing by two transposed digits. An embedding model, which scores meaning rather than characters, can rank the wrong one first. The assistant downstream then writes a confident, fluent answer about the wrong fix. Nobody sees a retrieval error. They see a wrong answer.

This is the standing argument for hybrid search: keep the vector index for meaning, add a keyword index for the strings that must match exactly, merge the two lists. The advice is usually asserted rather than measured, so we measured it, on a corpus we control, with the awkward queries left in.

The corpus was 373 chunks. Most of it is our own writing: 325 chunks cut from fifty of the posts on this blog. The rest is 48 operational records we wrote for the test: incident notes, part records, runbook owners, product notes, policies, host records, seeded with near-neighbours on purpose (error codes differing by transposed digits; a gasket for the P-9 pump and a near-identical one for the P-6; a Dana Whitfield and a Dana Whitmore who own different queues). Real corpora grow these confusions on their own. We planted ours where we could see them.

Thirty-two queries, written and frozen before anything ran. Twelve were exact-term lookups: a bare code, a part number, a name. Ten were paraphrases of passages in our posts, worded to share as little vocabulary with the passage as we could manage. Ten were mixed: an exact term inside a real question, or a choice between two confusables. Each query has exactly one correct chunk, and we scored every method on whether that chunk came back in the top five, and at what rank.

Three retrievers over the same chunks. Vector search with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, cosine similarity. BM25, the keyword ranking function, in a small implementation we wrote for the test (k1 = 1.5, b = 0.75). And a hybrid: reciprocal rank fusion with k = 60, merging the two top-50 lists. No reranker and no query rewriting: we wanted the retrieval layer's own behaviour, not a pipeline's.

The rig: 373 chunks in one corpus, two retrievers over it, and one fused list from reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60).

On the exact-term queries, BM25 was perfect: the correct record at rank one, twelve times out of twelve. A code is not a topic: it either matches or it doesn't, and a keyword index knows the difference between 1810 and 1180 in a way a vector does not.

Vector search never lost the record. The correct chunk sat in its top five every time, but a wrong near-neighbour took rank one in three of the twelve. ERR_AUTH_1180, a password-policy lockout, outranked ERR_AUTH_1810, the failover problem the query named. The P-6 pump's gasket outranked the P-9's. A connector error outranked the sync error. Each time, the right record sat at rank two. That sounds like a near miss and behaves like a failure, because the model downstream reads the top chunk first and builds on it — and the top chunk was a different incident with a different fix.

What each method returned for "AX-4410-B gasket", from the run output. The correct record is the P-9 gasket; vector search and the hybrid both put the P-6 gasket first.

On paraphrases the expected order flipped, then flattened. Vector search found the correct chunk in the top five for six of ten. BM25 managed four. The hybrid matched the vector score, six, and beat neither. If your traffic is mostly people asking questions in their own words, this test gives you no accuracy reason to run a second index.

The worst miss was shared. One question (how a system cautiously tests whether a failed tool has recovered before letting traffic back through) put the correct chunk at rank 126 under vector search and rank 76 under BM25. The hybrid never saw it at all: fusion only merges what the two retrievers surface, and neither surfaced it in fifty places. Asked about the same chunk with the words "circuit breaker" in the question, BM25 and the hybrid both returned it at rank one. The distance between those two outcomes is vocabulary, not meaning, and no blend closes it. Fusion did pull three buried answers closer — vector ranks 13, 25 and 22 became 7, 13 and 15 — still outside the five results a model actually reads. We count that as no rescue.

The mixed queries are where the hybrid earned its keep: ten of ten correct chunks in the top five, matching BM25 and ahead of vector search's eight. Across all 32 queries it found 28, against 26 for either method alone. That is the honest headline: a modest, real gain, concentrated where the two signals overlap.

But fusion is an average of two opinions, and it can talk a certain answer down. Twice on exact-term queries (the P-9 gasket; ERR_AUTH_1810) BM25 held the right record at rank one and the fused list demoted it to rank two, because the vector list preferred the neighbour. Our read: run the hybrid as the default, but let an exact match on a code-shaped token outrank the fusion when one fires. A part number is not a vote. That rule is a judgment from this data, not a property of the method.

The cost is not query time. On this rig a vector query took about 9 milliseconds and our from-scratch BM25 scan about 24, numbers that say more about a teaching implementation than about a production inverted index. The real cost is a second index to build, keep in step with the first, and interrogate at 2 a.m. when an answer is wrong and two rankings might be to blame.

Pay it when the corpus carries identifiers: tickets, parts catalogues, policy documents, logs, anything where users paste strings that must match character for character. That describes most production corpora we meet. Postpone it for a pure prose corpus of questions and explanations, where our paraphrase results say the second index buys complexity and returns nothing at the top of the list.

Thirty-two queries is a direction, not a significance test. One embedding model, and a small one; a larger model may blur codes less, or blur them differently. Our 48 records were written to be confusable on purpose. Real corpora are too, but rarely so neatly. And at 373 chunks every retriever is effectively scanning the whole haystack; at a million chunks the dynamics change. What survives those caveats is the shape of the result: keyword search owns exact strings, vector search owns paraphrase, and a blend buys the overlap while importing a demotion problem you have to design around.

Retrieval is usually the first layer we audit in a RAG deployment, because its failures arrive disguised as the model's. If your assistant answers confidently from almost-the-right record, send us the corpus and the questions it keeps missing through Trida AI's intake, and we will show you which layer is actually failing.

#9642. How would you design an E2E testing strategy using Playwright to comprehensively validate an SPA's error boundaries and

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at styrow.dev

⚠️ Mastering SPA Resilience: Playwright E2E for Error Boundaries How do you truly validate an SPA's graceful degradation and error recovery using Playwright, beyond just unit tests?

📌 Problem Statement Modern Single Page Applications (SPAs) critically depend on robust client-side error handling and error boundaries to prevent full application crashes. While unit tests verify individual error boundary components, a comprehensive End-to-End (E2E) strategy with Playwright is essential. It validates these mechanisms within the complete application context, including routing, data flows, and user interactions.

• The Core Challenge: Reliably inducing specific client-side errors and verifying the application's visual and functional response under controlled conditions.

❌ Antipattern: Relying solely on isolated unit tests which miss real-world interactions and cascading failures.

✅ Robust E2E Strategy: • Controlled Error Injection: Deliberately trigger JavaScript runtime errors or simulate API failures. • State Observation & Assertion: Verify error fallback UI presence, content, and proper functionality blocking. • Recovery Validation: Test if the application can recover (e.g., via a retry button) if applicable.

💡 Solution & Code Walkthrough Let's design a Playwright test to induce a client-side JavaScript runtime error and verify the SPA's error boundary. We'll use page.evaluate() to inject a fault.

Scenario: An important DataFetcher component should trigger an error boundary if its critical logic fails during rendering or an event.

🔑 Key Takeaways • ✅ Controlled Injection: Use page.evaluate() for client-side JS errors. For network errors, page.route() is ideal. • ✅ Comprehensive Validation: Assert the error boundary's visual presence, specific messages, and the state of critical UI elements. • ✅ Real-World Scenarios: Ensure your E2E tests cover complex user flows that might trigger hidden error paths. • ❌ Avoid Flakiness: Design your error injection precisely to target specific components or logic without side effects.

❓ Quick Summary Q&A • Q: Why E2E for error boundaries? A: To validate the full user experience, graceful degradation, and recovery within the complete application context. • Q: How to induce client-side JS errors? A: page.evaluate() is powerful for injecting code that forces runtime errors. • Q: What should E2E tests verify? A: Presence of error fallback UI, correct error messages, blocked functionality, and successful recovery (if a retry mechanism exists).

TAGS: playwright, e2e testing, spa, error handling, javascript, frontend testing, quality assurance

#9640. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

#9638. Capacitor for Beginners: Turn Your Web App Into a Mobile App

Capacitor lets you take a web app — the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript you already know — and run it as a native app on iOS and Android. You do not rewrite your app. You wrap it in a native shell and add access to native features like the camera, storage, and push notifications through plugins.

Capacitor is made by the Ionic team, and it works with any web framework — React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, or plain JavaScript. Your web code runs in a native WebView, and Capacitor's bridge lets JavaScript call native code and get results back.

Here is how you add it to an existing web project:

After that, your built web files live inside a real iOS and Android project that you open in Xcode or Android Studio. Native features are one import away:

That single call opens the native camera on the phone — no platform-specific code from you.

To start, build any small web app first — a notes app, a calculator, a weather page — then add Capacitor to it. Run it on a real device or an emulator to see your web code behave like a real app.

Capacitor is a great fit if you already have a web app and want a mobile version without learning native development or maintaining two codebases. It is also a good choice for teams that ship on web and mobile from one codebase.

The limits are real. Heavy graphics and animations can feel slower in a WebView than in a fully native app. Some native features need custom plugins if no official one exists. And you still need a Mac to build for iOS, which is Apple's rule, not Capacitor's.

Take a web app you already built and wrap it with Capacitor this weekend. Seeing your own project open on your phone as a real app is the fastest way to understand what it offers.
