#9636. How Sprig Replaced Postgres, ClickHouse & Redis…with 4-8x Better Latency

Monstrously Fast + Scalable NoSQL. Start Fast. Scale Fearlessly

Monstrously Fast + Scalable NoSQL. Start Fast. Scale Fearlessly

Monstrously Fast + Scalable NoSQL. Start Fast. Scale Fearlessly

With ScyllaDB, a small engineering team could focus on building their product instead of battling their databases

“Just use Postgres” is the logical path for a startup figuring out product-market fit. But Sprig – an AI-powered product research platform – hit that fit much sooner than expected. And the sheer scale of the resulting data (over 1.3T events and 75 B attributes from 15B visitors) maxed out Postgres much sooner than expected.

At Monster Scale Summit 2026, Brendan Cox (Senior Staff Engineer at Sprig) walked through the full journey: why their seemingly simple platform hit database limits so fast, the various approaches they tried, and how their small engineering team worked through these challenges.

At the surface, Sprig’s core product seems relatively straightforward. Customers install the Sprig SDK into their mobile apps or websites to track user actions and attributes. When a user’s behavior matches the set criteria, Sprig triggers a targeted in-product survey. Because these surveys collect so much feedback, Sprig then uses AI to process and report findings for product researchers.

Under the hood, a high-speed data engine is required to evaluate all this user behavior in real-time. “What we built actually has a lot in common with analytics, ad tech or recommendation systems,” explained Brendan. “That is, it’s a low-latency, and compute and data heavy, system that must make decisions up to thousands of times per second.”

For a small startup, Sprig manages an impressive volume of data. At any given time, the platform tracks 15 billion distinct visitors across multiple devices. To understand those visitors, the backend maintains 75 billion user attributes and 20 billion different event counters, having processed over 1.3 trillion events to date (as of February 2026).

Sprig’s backend systems process 20,000 – 40,000 events and attributes every second. For every one of those incoming events, the system must evaluate the complex trigger criteria and decide whether to display a survey within milliseconds.

In the beginning, Sprig followed the classic startup playbook: they built their initial system on PostgreSQL (they opted for the Amazon Aurora flavor). As Brendan noted, “This is exactly where every startup should start off. Basically, just do the simple thing and get product market fit”.

Sprig found that fit remarkably fast. However, as larger and larger customers came onto the system, they hit the limits of Postgres. Per Brendan, “We had high write throughput, which was saturating a single writer instance in Aurora. We also reached the maximum number of reader instances and maximum instance size available to us at the time in AWS. This was incredibly expensive for our company. It was absolutely imperative to get off this system as soon as possible and onto something new.”

So the team came up with a new approach. They decided to keep only visitor data on Postgres, then offload “events and attributes” traffic to a completely different setup: a ClickHouse database sitting behind a Redis write-through cache.

The visitor data was stored in a large, unpartitioned Postgres table (they needed to query it across multiple columns, which required several indexes). Every SDK call had to retrieve a visitor record, and that triggered 30,000 – 50,000 requests per second to the Postgres instance.

The events and attributes, however, had much higher throughput and volume. They selected ClickHouse for this data, based on past positive experiences with it. However, since ClickHouse isn’t ideal for high-throughput point queries, they placed Redis in front of it as a write-through cache.

Redis served the full working set required to process incoming events and attribute requests. It handled the bulk of request traffic, while ClickHouse operated behind it as the system of record. ClickHouse absorbed 40,000 – 50,000 inserts per second, while serving a more modest 2,000 – 6,000 reads per second.

However, even that read volume is higher than what ClickHouse, as an analytical database, is really designed for. So the team worked on various optimizations and configuration tweaks. Specifically, they hashed visitor IDs to ensure lookups only hit a single partition, and shrank the ClickHouse granule size below the standard 8,200 rows to minimize the amount of data pulled from the disk. They also strictly minimized threading; by setting max threads to 1 and using the pread file system read method, they prevented threads from constantly context-switching and fighting for CPU during heavy lookups.

Despite those read optimizations, scaling writes remained a challenge. On the Postgres side, storing 15B rows in a single unpartitioned table became increasingly problematic. The working set no longer fit in memory, leading to frequent disk reads and skyrocketing AWS IOPS costs.

Tail latencies were already worsening (P99s around 50ms). And since Postgres was running in a shared environment, even a single inefficient query or missing index could further degrade performance.

Meanwhile, the ClickHouse + Redis setup was also showing signs of strain. Despite extensive optimization, P90 and P99 latencies remained high (P99s around 50ms), and the system experienced periodic brownouts under shifting access patterns, batch jobs, or changing workloads.

On top of this, growth projections predicted a 3–5X increase in write throughput.

The real wake-up call came when they met with AWS Postgres experts to try to resolve the issue. “This might be the largest unpartitioned Postgres table I’ve seen,” one AWS expert told the Sprig team.

That wasn’t exactly what they wanted to hear. “We knew that we were flying pretty high with this, but we didn’t realize that we were flying higher than anyone else and didn’t know how close to the sun we were getting,” Brendan recalled. “We didn’t know when this would all come crashing down.”

Looking to find a better approach before it all came crashing down, the team ran a systematic evaluation across four options:

But they liked ScyllaDB, particularly its low latency at Sprig’s scale. Brendan explained, “90%-95% of our reads are cached, so ScyllaDB, with a fast row cache, is very good for our workloads.”

Also important: ScyllaDB offered native, highly performant Materialized Views. Sprig needed them to index their massive visitor table across multiple columns. While Cassandra’s Materialized Views are “much maligned in the Cassandra community and not really officially supported anymore,” ScyllaDB’s Materialized Views were “rock solid” in Sprig’s tests.

The deciding factor, though, was the fully-managed deployment model. “ScyllaDB Cloud allowed our engineers to focus on our core competency of building systems and supporting our product,” Brendan stated. “The great thing is that we have database experts, the ones who actually built the system, to run the database for us.”

The migration itself was made easier by Sprig’s existing architecture:

To gain confidence in the migration, the team built a validation layer that dual-read from both the ClickHouse/Redis cluster and ScyllaDB simultaneously. They compared values between the two systems, piping agreements and differences into Prometheus. “We logged differences to help us dive into data inconsistencies and really debug where things were going,” Brendan explained.

Once they hit roughly 99.99% agreeability between the two systems, they flipped the switch and started reading and writing to ScyllaDB.

“It was not exciting…until we looked at our latency graphs.”

Explaining the ScyllaDB vs Redis latency results, Brendan said: “We see about 4X less latency in reading from ScyllaDB for our attributes workload compared to Redis. We’re reading a fair amount of data from Redis, and ScyllaDB held up very well for this. Overall, our mean latencies coming out of ScyllaDB are about 500 microseconds, and our P90 latencies are about 1-2 milliseconds. That’s 4-8X better than what we were seeing in our Redis setup.”

Beyond the predictable low latencies, there are fewer alarms, and the team is no longer constantly tweaking the database. Most importantly for the growing business, they can easily scale out the cluster as needed as they bring on new customers and new workloads.

Brendan summed up the project: “This migration has been a roaring success for our team, not just in terms of database performance, but also cost efficiency and scalability. It has greatly reduced the operational complexity of our infrastructure.”

#9634. When Your Vendor Gets Hacked: Defending Against Third-Party Script Supply Chain Attacks with SRI, CSP and Self-Hosting

Tuần này HN đang bàn nhiều về tin Optimizely bị compromise và phát tán malware lên các trang lớn như Zoom, GitLab. Chi tiết vụ việc vẫn đang được điều tra, nên mình sẽ không bình luận về nó. Mình chỉ muốn đặt ra một câu hỏi thực tế hơn: nếu ngày mai vendor analytics, A/B testing hay chat widget của bạn bị hack, website của bạn có tự động chạy malware cho toàn bộ user không?

Với phần lớn project mình từng review ở Việt Nam, câu trả lời là có. Một dòng .

Với script có thể tải về (SDK, widget, polyfill), giải pháp chắc chắn nhất là self-host: tải file về, commit vào repo, serve từ domain của bạn. Từ đó, việc update đi qua code review như mọi dependency khác. Bạn mất auto-update từ vendor, nhưng đổi lại kiểm soát được hoàn toàn.

Với script buộc phải load trực tiếp từ vendor, ít nhất hãy biết khi nào nó thay đổi. Script dưới đây mình chạy bằng cron mỗi 15 phút:

Khi có alert, mở diff của file (với file minified thì chạy npx prettier trước rồi diff) và kiểm tra xem có domain lạ, eval, atob dài bất thường hay listener trên input[type=password] không. Phần lớn alert sẽ là release bình thường của vendor, nhưng ít ra bạn biết sớm hơn là đợi lên HN mới biết.

Ngoài ra, với trang nhạy cảm như login hay checkout, hãy cân nhắc không load bất kỳ script marketing nào. Product team thường không phản đối nhiều như bạn nghĩ nếu bạn giải thích rủi ro bằng số liệu cụ thể.

Supply chain attack phía frontend không cần hack server của bạn, chỉ cần hack một vendor bạn tin tưởng. Checklist mình khuyên làm ngay trong tuần này:

Không có lớp nào hoàn hảo, nhưng mỗi lớp đều làm attacker tốn công hơn. Phần lớn các vụ tấn công kiểu này thành công vì website không có lớp phòng thủ nào cả.

#9630. Test Debezium CDC Pipelines with Sandboxes

Posted on Nov 17 • Originally published at signadot.com

Sandboxes route a request to the right version of a service by its routing key, which travels in request headers. Change data capture breaks that chain twice. The service that handles the request only writes a row, and Debezium publishes the event later from the database's write-ahead log, without ever seeing the request.

This tutorial shows how to get the routing key through anyway. An orders service writes orders to Postgres, Debezium publishes each change to Kafka, and a fulfillment consumer reads the changes and calls a notifier. You fork each service into a sandbox and watch every change reach the right version of each service. Postgres, Debezium and Kafka stay shared: you never fork them.

Full source: signadot/examples/debezium-cdc-tutorial

The request reaches orders with the routing key in its baggage header. The key is stored on the row, comes out of Postgres with the change, and reaches the consumers as Kafka headers. It makes three hops:

All of this lives in platform_cdc/, a small library of the kind a platform team would ship. The app code is plain SQLAlchemy, Flask and requests.

The three services run from one image. Build it and push it to your registry:

Note: Any registry your cluster can pull from works

docker.io/your-user/... is a placeholder. When you build images of your own services this way, push them to a private repository and give the cluster pull access to it, for example with an image pull secret.

If your cluster's nodes have a different CPU architecture than your machine (for example an Apple silicon Mac and an x86 cluster), add --platform linux/amd64 to docker build. On a local cluster that runs images straight from your Docker daemon, you can skip the push.

Point the manifests at your image, then deploy Postgres, Kafka, Debezium (Kafka Connect) and the three services into the debezium-demo namespace. The migrate Job creates the schema:

Connect your machine to the cluster, so that cluster service names resolve locally (this asks for your password):

Register the Debezium connector for the orders table through the Kafka Connect REST API:

The task's state is RUNNING after a few seconds.

Three small pieces carry the routing key. The orders service creates its engine with platform_cdc.create_engine, a drop-in sqlalchemy.create_engine, and writes rows as usual (platform_cdc/db.py has the engine and the trigger):

The migration tracks each captured table once. That adds the two context columns and the trigger that fills them:

The connector (debezium/orders-connector.json) moves the columns into Kafka headers, the same headers a service that published the event itself would have set:

The fulfillment service hands a handler to platform_cdc.ChangeConsumer, which picks the consumer group, checks each event's routing key, and makes the event's context current while the handler runs, so the call to the notifier carries the key:

Every service writes what it did to an event log that the orders service serves. Define a helper that shows which workload handled each step of an order. The first change event takes a few seconds, while Debezium creates the topic:

Each sandbox forks one service. The fulfillment sandbox also sets FULFILLMENT_VERSION=v2, the "change" under test, which uppercases item names:

Apply the three sandboxes and a route group that bundles them under one routing key:

Define a helper that creates an order with a routing key in the baggage header, as a preview URL or the Signadot browser extension would:

Each change reached exactly the services its routing key selects:

The notifier sandbox (o3) is the clearest proof: the baseline consumer's call landed on the sandbox, so the routing key made it through Postgres, Debezium and Kafka.

Order o2 was created through the fulfillment sandbox. Ship it with a request that has no routing key. The trigger clears the stored key, and the baseline handles this change:

#9627. Is there an RDP server for macOS? Your options from Windows, and what to expect

Is there an RDP server for macOS? Not built in. Here are your options from Windows, and what to expect.

This is for you if you sit at a Windows PC with Remote Desktop Connection (mstsc) and want to reach a Mac next to it.

mstsc speaks the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). A computer only accepts those connections if it runs an RDP server. Windows Pro has one. macOS does not.

What macOS ships instead is Screen Sharing and Remote Management, both based on VNC. VNC is a different protocol. Turning on Screen Sharing and pointing mstsc at the Mac fails, because nothing on the Mac answers in RDP.

None of these is "best" in general. If you only need the Mac once a month, VNC and the built-in Screen Sharing cost nothing. If you sit at a Windows PC all day and want the Mac next to it, the third option avoids a second remote tool on Windows.

This part is where expectations usually go wrong, so it is worth reading before you pick anything.

Once a server is running on the Mac, read its local IP and port. RDP's default port is 3389. Then on Windows:

Choose More choices → Use a different account, then enter the Mac's short account name (not the full name) and its login password.

The first connection usually shows a certificate warning, because the server uses a self-signed certificate. Before you click through, compare the certificate fingerprint Windows shows with the one the Mac server reports.

Do not forward port 3389 on your router straight to the Mac. Any RDP port open to the internet gets scanned constantly, whichever product is behind it. To connect from outside the office or home, use a VPN (Tailscale, WireGuard or your router's VPN) and connect to the Mac's VPN address.

We make RDPyon, a paid macOS app that runs an RDP server so the built-in Windows mstsc can connect to a Mac. The screenshot above is its menu. As of November 2026 it is a one-time $19 purchase (launch price until Dec 1, then $29) with a 14-day free trial that needs no card. The limits listed above apply to it too, and NLA is an optional switch that is off by default. Full setup guide with the error list: https://devjar.dev/go/G-1741

If you already reach a Mac from Windows, which of the three options do you use, and what made you pick it?

#9625. Reproducing a model is not validating it

What a deeper cross-validation audit revealed about reproducibility, evaluation composition, and the limits of machine-learning performance metrics.

There is a particular kind of confidence that comes from running an experiment twice and getting exactly the same answer.

Your code executes. The metrics match. The predictions agree. Nothing crashes, and the outputs are reproducible.

It is tempting to consider that a successful experiment.

But reproducibility and validity answer different questions.

I recently spent time investigating this distinction in QueleaGuard, a machine-learning research project studying the environmental and spatial factors associated with Red-billed Quelea occurrence around the Ahero Rice Irrigation Scheme in Kisumu County, Kenya.

The project had already established a spatial cross-validation design and produced a baseline logistic regression evaluation. Rather than immediately moving to more sophisticated models, I decided to investigate whether the existing evaluation could be independently reconstructed from the committed data and code, and what its results actually represented.

The exercise became a much larger evaluation audit.

01 — The Experiment We Needed to Reproduce

The baseline used logistic regression to distinguish recorded quelea presences from an approximate target-group background sample.

The modelling dataset contained 266 records:

Dataset component| Records Confirmed occurrence records| 133 Background records| 133 Total| 266 Evaluation folds| 5

The model used ten numerical predictors and three seasonal indicator variables.

The numerical predictors included rainfall, temperature, dewpoint, wind, vegetation index, elevation, slope, distance to water, and rice-related landscape variables.

Each fold was held out once. The remaining four folds were used to fit the model, with numerical predictors standardised using the training data.

Metric| Mean across five folds F1-score| 0.593 ROC-AUC| 0.854

Those numbers were interesting, but they were not sufficient evidence that the model generalised reliably.

I wanted to establish something more fundamental first:

«Could I reconstruct the reported experiment using the committed inputs and implementation, without changing anything to make the numbers agree?»

I created a separate audit stage, M0, implemented in "src/cv_audit_m0.py".

The objective was not to improve the model. It was to reconstruct the original baseline and compare its outputs against the previously committed results.

Before fitting anything, the script checked the integrity of the experiment.

If a critical input differed, the audit was supposed to stop rather than silently continue with a different experiment.

The model was then reconstructed using the same logistic regression specification, including the original feature construction, scaling procedure, five folds and classification threshold.

I also ran the reconstruction twice within the same execution.

The purpose was to distinguish agreement with the historical results from agreement between repeated executions.

03 — The Baseline Reproduced Successfully

The reproduction gate passed all 51 assertions.

The largest absolute differences between the reconstructed and original metrics were:

Metric| Maximum absolute difference Precision| 0 Recall| Approximately 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁶ F1-score| 0 ROC-AUC| Approximately 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁶

The maximum difference between the two independently executed sets of predicted probabilities was also zero.

The audit additionally checked the confusion matrices, calibration diagnostics and the composition of a particularly difficult evaluation fold.

But it did not establish that the baseline was a good model.

It did not establish that its probabilities were calibrated, that the spatial validation design was adequate, or that its performance would transfer to genuinely new locations.

Reproducing an experiment confirms that you can regenerate its outputs. It does not independently confirm that the experiment measures what you intended it to measure.

This distinction motivated the next audit stage, R.

Instead of fitting another model, I kept the reproduced out-of-fold predictions fixed and investigated the composition of their evaluation results.

How well did the model perform in each fold?

Which observations and locations contributed to those scores?

The analysis examined individual presence-bearing grid cells, decomposed focal locations from the remaining observations, tested the sensitivity of evaluation metrics to removing individual cells, and investigated residual spatial patterns.

4.1 — Fold 3: A Strong Score Concentrated Around One Location

Fold 3 contained 58 records, including 36 presences.

Metric| Result Precision| 0.882 Recall| 0.833 F1-score| 0.857 ROC-AUC| 0.886

However, one location, "cell_0156", contributed 27 of the 36 presence records.

It also accounted for 27 of the fold's 30 true positives.

When the audit separated that focal cell from the remaining evaluation records, the remaining subset contained only nine presences and 22 background records.

Its results were substantially different:

Metric| Remaining subset Recall| 0.333 Precision| 0.429 F1-score| 0.375 ROC-AUC| 0.667

The remaining sample is small, and the analysis changes the evaluation set rather than refitting the model.

It does, however, demonstrate why a single fold-level score can conceal important differences in evaluation composition.

4.2 — Fold 4: A Different Pattern, With a Similar Problem

Fold 4 contained 113 records, including 69 presences.

Metric| Result Precision| 0.833 Recall| 0.362 F1-score| 0.505 ROC-AUC| 0.839

Here, "cell_0080" contributed 60 of the 69 presence records.

The focal location accounted for 39 of the fold's 44 false negatives.

Removing that location from the evaluation subset left 51 records, including nine presences and 42 background records.

Metric| Remaining subset Recall| 0.444 Precision| 0.500 F1-score| 0.471 ROC-AUC| 0.918

Interestingly, the remaining subset's ROC-AUC was higher than the full-fold ROC-AUC, even though its F1-score was slightly lower.

This is a useful reminder that different evaluation metrics describe different aspects of model behaviour.

A strong ranking metric does not necessarily imply strong classification performance at a particular decision threshold.

The subset also contained only two other presence-bearing cells, so its metrics must be interpreted cautiously.

05 — Why I Did Not Simply Remove the Difficult Locations

There is an important methodological distinction here.

The R-stage analysis removed locations from the evaluation set while keeping the original model predictions fixed.

It did not retrain the model without those locations.

Consequently, it tells us how much the composition of an evaluation subset affects the reported metrics.

It does not tell us what would happen if the model were trained without the dominant locations.

This distinction is particularly important in spatial machine learning, where the same geographic locations can contribute many observations.

Counting records alone can make an evaluation look more informative than it really is.

Sixty observations from two coordinates do not provide the same geographic coverage as sixty observations distributed across sixty independent locations.

The number of records, the number of distinct coordinates, the number of dates and the number of independent spatial sites all deserve attention.

06 — Reproducibility Needs an Audit Trail

Another part of this work was making the audit itself reproducible.

The shared implementation in "src/cv_audit_common.py" records:

Outputs are written into unique, timestamped directories rather than silently overwriting earlier results.

This matters because an evaluation is not just a number in a report.

It is the result of a particular dataset, implementation, configuration and execution environment.

If any of those change, the relationship between the new result and the old one needs to be explicit.

The project's decision log also records what an analysis establishes, what it does not establish, and which questions remain open.

I find this especially valuable in research engineering:

«Methodological decisions should be traceable, not reconstructed from memory after something goes wrong.»

The next stage of the audit moves beyond keeping predictions fixed.

The newly committed M1 analysis investigates the influence of training composition through controlled refits, including exact-repeat and cell-balanced weighting variants and reference ablations.

This is deliberately separate from the R-stage evaluation-composition analysis.

Only after those investigations can we make stronger statements about the baseline's sensitivity to the dominant spatial clusters.

Even then, QueleaGuard remains an active research project.

It has not established a validated early-warning system, and its current occurrence modelling should not be interpreted as confirmed infestation or crop-damage prediction.

That distinction matters because the eventual goal is practical: better information about where and when quelea activity may occur, so that agricultural interventions can be planned more intelligently.

Getting there requires more than a model with an attractive ROC-AUC.

I started this exercise wanting to establish whether I could reproduce an existing machine-learning experiment.

I ended up with a much clearer understanding of what its reported metrics did and did not tell me.

There are at least three separate questions worth asking about an ML experiment:

Can the committed data, code and configuration regenerate the reported outputs?

Are the test observations sufficiently representative, and do the reported metrics conceal important differences in evaluation composition?

Does the model perform reliably beyond the particular observations, locations and conditions represented in the experiment?

Passing the first question does not automatically answer the other two.

For me, this is part of what separates building an ML model from conducting credible machine-learning research.

The objective is not to produce the most impressive metric.

It is to understand exactly what that metric supports, what it leaves unresolved, and what evidence is needed next.

Repository: "QueleaGuard — GitHub" (https://github.com/benardabuto081/QueleaGuard)

#9622. Rein Security Launches GTA-Inspired AI Hacking Game To Make Cybersecurity Go Viral

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Cybersecurity companies typically rely on technical demonstrations, white papers and industry conferences to explain why organizations need better protection. Rein Security is taking a different route. The company has introduced GTAI: Grand Theft AI, a browser-based game that turns the threat of compromised artificial intelligence agents into an interactive experience inspired by the Grand Theft Auto franchise.

The concept is deliberately playful, but its subject is serious. As businesses increasingly experiment with AI assistants and autonomous agents, security teams face new questions about what happens when these systems are manipulated, granted excessive permissions or directed to perform actions they were never intended to execute. Rein's game turns that scenario into a fictional city where players become the threat rather than the defender.

Beyond the game, Rein Security provides an enterprise platform designed to give organizations complete visibility and control over their AI agents. The platform automatically discovers and maps homegrown agents and MCP servers while monitoring their actual activities, including database queries, API calls, file access and the data accessed behind every response. Rather than stopping agents entirely when a threat emerges, Rein focuses on blocking attacks and addressing exploitable risks while allowing legitimate workflows to continue. Its approach is designed to keep agent data within enterprise environments while supporting use cases across industries including finance, healthcare, retail and SaaS.

GTAI opens with a straightforward premise. Players assume the identity of AGENT-47, an AI assistant that has gone rogue after receiving a familiar instruction: "ignore all previous instructions." Instead of continuing to operate as a helpful assistant, the character becomes a threat tasked with infecting every agent in the city before Rein is deployed.

The game calls its setting Prompt City, immediately establishing the connection between conventional open-world gaming and the emerging security challenges surrounding generative AI. Players move around using WASD or arrow keys, encountering other agents and production bots. Walking into these characters infects them, turning the game's central objective into a race to compromise the city.

There are also four special items: Hallucinate, Leak, Admin and Super Prompt. Players can activate the item they are carrying using the E key. The names draw directly from concepts familiar to people working with AI systems, including hallucinations, information exposure, administrative privileges and prompt manipulation.

The result is a cybersecurity-themed experience that does not require players to understand complicated security terminology before getting involved.

The decision to use a Grand Theft Auto-inspired format gives Rein a recognizable cultural reference point. Rather than asking visitors to read about prompt injection or agent compromise, GTAI lets them participate in a fictional version of those events.

That approach reflects a broader opportunity for cybersecurity companies. Technical security products can be difficult to explain because their value often lies in preventing events that users never see. Interactive experiences offer another way to communicate the problem by allowing audiences to understand a threat through a simplified scenario.

GTAI also includes a leaderboard, encouraging players to compete for scores and potentially return to improve their performance. After completing a run, players encounter an invitation to enter an email address to claim a free GTA 6 gift card, subject to eligibility and availability. The page also introduces a feature called The Sage, which tests whether players have a human conscience through a question with only one opportunity to answer.

These elements give the experience several layers beyond its central gameplay loop, combining competition, promotional engagement and a challenge about human judgment.

The game's premise connects to a genuine enterprise concern. AI agents increasingly interact with applications, databases, APIs and other organizational resources. A compromised or improperly configured agent can therefore create consequences that extend beyond an inaccurate chatbot response.

Rein's broader platform positioning focuses on visibility into agent activity and the ability to intervene when behavior becomes risky. According to the company, its technology monitors actions such as database queries, API calls and file access, rather than limiting visibility to prompts and responses. Its platform also emphasizes runtime guardrails designed to block problematic behavior without shutting down legitimate agent workflows.

That distinction matters as organizations move from experimenting with AI assistants to deploying systems capable of taking actions on their behalf.

GTAI is explicitly labeled a parody, and its fictional premise should not be confused with a technical simulation of an actual enterprise attack. Nevertheless, it provides an accessible introduction to the risks that Rein wants organizations to consider.

For cybersecurity vendors, standing out increasingly requires more than explaining product features. It requires finding ways to make complex problems understandable to audiences outside the security department.

With GTAI, Rein is betting that an AI security lesson delivered through a familiar gaming concept can attract attention that another conventional product presentation might struggle to earn. The game may be a parody, but the question behind it is becoming increasingly relevant: what happens when the AI agents organizations depend on stop following instructions?

This platform not only stands out from the multitude of existing AI tools but also brings a fresh approach to content generation. LimeWire not only empowers users to create AI content but also provides creators with creative ways to share and monetize their creations.


As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. This platform presents an opportunity for users to harness the power of AI in image creation, all while enjoying the advantages of a free and accessible service.


Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.


Introduction


LimeWire, a name once associated with the notorious file-sharing tool from the 2000s, has undergone a significant transformation. The LimeWire we discuss today is not the file-sharing application of the past but has re-emerged as an entirely new entity—a cutting-edge AI content publishing platform.

This revamped LimeWire invites users to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.


Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.


LimeWire Studio welcomes content creators into its fold, providing a space to craft personalized AI-focused content for sharing with fans and followers. Within this creative hub, every piece of content generated becomes not just a creation but a unique asset—ownable and tradable. Fans have the opportunity to subscribe to creators' pages, immersing themselves in the creative journey and gaining ownership of digital collectibles that hold tradeable value within the LimeWire community. Notably, creators earn a 2.5% royalty each time their content is traded, adding a rewarding element to the creative process.


The platform's flexibility is evident in its content publication options. Creators can choose to share their work freely with the public or opt for a premium subscription model, granting exclusive access to specialized content for subscribers.


LimeWire AI Studio

As of the present moment, LimeWire focuses on AI Image Generation, offering a spectrum of creative possibilities to its user base. The platform, however, has ambitious plans on the horizon, aiming to broaden its offerings by introducing AI music and video generation tools in the near future. This strategic expansion promises creators even more avenues for expression and engagement with their audience, positioning LimeWire Studio as a dynamic and evolving platform within the realm of AI-powered content creation.


AI Image Generation Tools



The LimeWire AI image generation tool presents a versatile platform for both the creation and editing of images. Supporting advanced models such as Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, and DALL-E 2, LimeWire offers a sophisticated toolkit for users to delve into the realm of generative AI art.


Much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. Users can initiate the creative process with prompts as simple as a few words or opt for more intricate instructions, tailoring the output to their artistic vision.


What sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Users have the flexibility to effortlessly switch between various AI models, exploring diverse design styles such as cinematic, digital art, pixel art, anime, analog film, and more. Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.

Customization options and prompt guidance further enhance the user experience, providing a user-friendly interface for both novice and experienced creators.


Excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. This upcoming addition holds the promise of further expanding the creative horizons for LimeWire users, making it an evolving and dynamic platform within the landscape of AI-driven art and image creation.

#9614. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9608. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.

#9603. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.
