#9584. 11 Best Classic American Candy Stores Across The US

There's hardly a saying that expresses unbridled joy like "kid in a candy store." But why do kids get all the fun? Candy stores, those brightly colored meccas of sky-high sugar intake, beckon many Americans far into adulthood. Candy, after all, is one of those food products that can really take us back, so candy stores are capable of injecting a sense of nostalgia, childlike reverie, and excitement into anyone's day.

Candy has long been a staple of American culture, with the oldest candy stores in the United States stretching back into past centuries. In the modern world, however, candy enthusiasts keep tabs on their favorite indulgences through candy-focused blogs, sweets-obsessed Instagram accounts, and TikTok viral candy sensations. Meanwhile, towns, states, and even nationwide publications regularly hold contests for the best candy store in the area (or in the country). These sources, and more, inspired this list of the coolest candy stores in the United States.

And in a society where more is more, candy stores have evolved from quaint little shops (still worth a visit for transporting yourself to the past) to mega-sized outlets overflowing with sweets. Some have blossomed into department store-level or warehouse-like square footage, others have added attractions far beyond the candy itself, from mini golf to candy museums, and some are just old-time-tastic. The candy stores listed here are not just the perfect places to get your candy fix. They've become must-visit destinations for travelers around the country.

Philadelphia's Shane Confectionery is one of America's oldest candy stores — in fact, it's the oldest continuously operated confectionery. The company emphasizes that this claim to fame means that its operation has been consistently making and selling confections longer than any other site in America, in a historic four-story brick building that's survived for over 150 years.

But it wasn't until 1910, when the company was sold to Edward R. Shane, that many of the retail shop's intricate, old-fashioned design elements were put into place. As the company explains, Shane installed elaborately carved cabinets, curved glass showcases, and marble countertops to highlight his confections, as well as stained glass transom windows above the storefront to allure passersby in front of his shop. Best of all, many of these architectural details have been restored and are on display in the shop today, making a visit there a bit like stepping into a charming bygone era.

It's no wonder that Eater Philadelphia has called Shane Confectionery the "time portal to Philadelphia's sugary past," calling out the efforts of current owners, brothers Ryan and Eric Berley, who breathed new life into the longstanding business in 2011. Fans regularly show it love online as a must-visit when living in or traveling through the City of Brotherly Love.

With enthusiastic reviews and a high rankings online, Sweet Pete's Candy in Jacksonville, Florida, is hailed as the largest candy store in the Southeast. And the setting can't be beat: Visit Jacksonville points out that it's located in a historic 22,000-square-foot mansion right in the heart of downtown. From sour candies to hand-pulled lollipops, Sweet Pete's has your candy cravings covered.

Sweet Pete's Candy also gets a leg up on the candy competition by serving customers with dietary restrictions. It offers an entire allergy-friendly array of candies, including a selection of gluten-free, dairy-free, vegan-friendly, and nut-free options. A classic treat is Pete's Famous Sea Salt Caramel, now available in different flavors, like Apple Pie.

Meanwhile, visitors can make a day out of their visit, because Sweet Pete's also houses Fizzies & Fare, an in-house restaurant and bar that's touted by the company as home to hundreds of unique craft sodas, over-the-top Crazy Shakes, classic American eats, candy-inspired cocktails, and more. Candy fans can also learn how their favorite candies are made through a guided tour, led by one of the staff's "Candy Connoisseurs," through the three-story "candy mansion," then grab their own handmade custom chocolate bar fresh from Sweet Pete's kitchen. The business even hosts parties, events, field trips for local school kids, and classes on-site.

Sweet Mickey's, in the Ballard neighborhood of Seattle, is named after owner Randy Brinker's grandma and pays homage to her bygone party shop and homemade sweets. Many publications laud it as one of the best candy stores in the country, thanks to its variety of homemade fudges and truffles alongside classic candy favorites like Sugar Babies and international sensations like Danish salted licorice.

With a storefront tucked into the charming brick buildings of historic Ballard, it's the perfect place for a candy store with a vintage vibe and an old-time Americana aesthetic. From handmade goodies to its carefully curated selection of traditional and artisanal sweets from around the globe, candy lovers (or even the pickiest of eaters) can find something for them.

Even better, this candy store has a heart. Since its 2012 grand opening, it has supported the local Little League, sponsored movie nights in the park, and hosted onsite parties and events to create sweet memories and build community.

It'Sugar, with candy-colored locations nationwide, was already known for its San Francisco flagship location, with a three-floor candy store in Fisherman's Wharf. The brand, with locations from coast to coast, then opened a 24,000-square-foot location in East Rutherford, New Jersey's American Dream shopping mall. This location, dubbed the World's First Candy Department Store, also spans three floors, though there are plenty across the country.

Some of its over-the-top features at the East Rutherford location include: a three-story-tall Statue of Liberty replica covered in more than 1.5 million Jelly Belly beans, an immersive lollipop garden filled with nearly 10,000 lollipops, dozens of branded shops like Sour Patch Kids, Swedish Fish, Nerds, Starburst, and Reese's. It's truly a candy lover's dream come true. YouTubers have hailed it as an amazing feat of candy awesomeness, all a stone's throw from New York City.

The brand It'Sugar calls itself a "retailtainer," a mashup of retailer and entertainment. As company lore explains, the brand was founded by candy veteran Jeff Rubin in 2006 and has grown to more than 120 locations throughout the United States and Canada. It's known for "absurd sugar innovations" and the Sugar High Club, with which loyal visitors can earn points for their purchases — then, of course, they can cash them in for more sugar.

Cleveland hosts North America's largest candy store, going strong for more than 75 years: b.a. Sweetie Candy Company. Cleveland.com calls it Cleveland's version of Willy Wonka's Candy Factory, and for good reason. Company stats boast that it hosts more than 500,000 visitors per year (making it one of the city's top attractions) and stocks more than 5,500 items in its wholesale store, to the tune of over $5 million in inventory on-hand at any given time.

With classic candy, retro candy, bulk candy, wholesale candy, and more, the store promises "the absolute largest variety of candy available anywhere in North America." Meaning, if you need 1,000 pounds of Tootsie Rolls to throw a parade, it's your outlet. It even keeps an eye on bygone favorites and claims it has been instrumental in bringing back vintage candies that had disappeared from shelves, including nostalgic names like Bonomo's Turkish Taffy, Slo Poke, Regal Crown, and Broadway licorice rolls.

All that would be enough to lure any candy fan, but b.a. Sweetie Candy Company is much more than just a candy store. It's a bona fide family-fun destination, offering Golfland Park, which has two 18-hole mini golf courses, complete with lights for evening play, koi ponds, a cascading waterfall, and concession stands. Meanwhile, the Soda Shoppe serves up homemade ice cream, sundaes, malts, and over 100 sodas in a barn-style parlor.

This New York City treasure actually started as a shoe and hat repair shop — but a little push cart outside also sold candy. According to company lore, in the Depression years, 1937, the business owners decided to focus on their biggest moneymaker, candy, and became known as Economy Candy. After World War II, Morris "Moishe" Cohen and his brother in law assumed ownership and expanded the business, selling candy, chocolate, gift baskets, dried fruit, nuts, and more. Morris' son, Jerry, and his wife, Ilene, took over after its move to the current location at 108 Rivington Street, then passed the business to son Mitchell, who runs it today.

In other words, this living legend is a true family affair — and a multigenerational sensation that has become a part of the rich history of New York City. In 2023, the northwest corner of Rivington and Essex Streets were co-named Morris "Moishe" Cohen Way in honor of Morris and Economy Candy's lasting legacies.

Today, the store still boasts over 2,000 items for sale, and visitors routinely rave about its massive selection and reasonable prices online. Hot sellers include chocolate-covered graham crackers (with and without jelly), chocolate-covered pretzels, jelly rings, gummies, and those hard-to-find candy bars. For those outside New York City, Economy Candy offers online sales, as well.

A candy shop with old-fashioned soda fountain treats like ice cream, specialty chocolate candies and fudge, more than 400 candies for buying in bulk, and 3,000-plus wrapped candies — all in colorful circus-theme surroundings? Yes, please.

The Big Top Candy Shop has been serving the Austin community (as well as candy-minded travelers) since 2007. Visitors praised its wall-to-wall candy selection, laid out in candy-colored rows, jars, racks, and even in a lollipop tree. Passing by Peanuts, the elephant pictured on the shop's entrance (facing the city's famed South Congress Avenue, known for housing quirky boutiques), visitors will find a whimsical wonderland at Big Top Candy with classic soda machines, retro candies, and a hefty bulk section customers can grab by the scoop.

The store promises both nostalgic favorites and new creations from around the globe. Whether you're just passing through for SXSW or a stalwart resident, Big Top Candy Shop is a must-visit in the Live Music Capital of the World.

Minnesota's Largest Candy Store in Jordan, Minnesota, nods to its mind-boggling mass of inventory in its very name — and the company would seem intent on living up to that moniker. Owned by Robert Wagner, and also known as Jim's Apple Farm, the store houses not only nostalgic candy, but fresh-baked pies and strudels, the world's largest selection of sodas, an array of popcorn flavors, and locally-sourced items (think pastas, jams, jellies, and even puzzles). These are all sourced from surrounding farms, making this Midwestern gem not only a candy emporium but a true shopping destination that supports locals and promotes Minnesota products to everyone who enters.

Fortunately, its location is relatively convenient for passers-through, as the store is only 35 miles from Minneapolis. And you can't miss it — the store is housed in a massive, bright yellow barn. It's a must-stop not only thanks to its dizzying array of sweet and savory treats, but fun touches throughout its interior decor, such as a new observatory-like dome featuring a mural with more than two dozen superheroes, an animatronic band, and a fortune-telling machine. Essentially, this Minnesota behemoth will bring out the kid in anyone.

20430 Johnson Memorial Dr, Jordan, MN 55352

Calling itself one of the oldest continuously operated, family-owned candy businesses in the U.S., Schimpff's Confectionery has been hailed as America's best candy store. It was also featured on a national television special "Disney Celebrates America: The Pursuit of Happiness."

With 135 years of history, Schimpff's Confectionery more than deserves those honors — its recipes and business stretch back to the 1800s. The company history notes that the recipe for its famous Cinnamon Red Hots were handwritten in the recipe book of Gustav "Gus" Schimpff Sr. back in 1891. And it's still making waves, having been featured on several shows and publications.

With such an illustrious history, it makes sense that Schimpff's Confectionery also houses a candy museum, with thousands of pieces of American candy memorabilia. The museum, along with a candy demonstration area, were added to an adjacent building in 2001, a dream child of 1990s-era owners Warren Schimpff and his wife Jill. Today, fifth-generation owners Steve and Beth Shepherd have taken the helm and embrace the time-honored traditions and recipes at Schimpff's Confectionery.

Seeking candy from the 1970s, or maybe your favorite candy from the 1990s? The Peppermint Stick Candy Store & Ice Cream Parlor in Boyertown, Pennsylvania, stocks a cornucopia of vintage candies alongside modern-day favorites and gourmet goodies like truffles. Whether you're visiting in-store or shopping online, this candy store has got you covered. In fact, its website has a handy online shopping feature, making it easy for customers to browse by decade.

Opened in 2015, this woman-owned business also offers Longacre's ice cream for indulgent sundaes and 20-ounce milkshakes, plus bakery delights like Ice Cream Nachos (waffle cones make the chips) and the Cinnamon Roll Sundae, and a Soda Jerk menu with soda fountain favorites. Customers will find not just a store, but an unforgettable experience at The Peppermint Stick Candy Store & Ice Cream Parlor. They can find fudge, artisan chocolates, loose chocolates, gummy candy, penny candy, nostalgic candy, gourmet truffles (in flavors like mint, Champagne, tiramisu, and key lime), and even a penny candy section. Basically, if you leave hungry, you've done something wrong.

26 E Philadelphia Ave, Boyertown, PA 19512

Since 1934, Bright's Candies has been whipping up candy the old-fashioned way. Even now, this destination features charming equipment to make its treats, including large copper kettles, metal candy molds, and an antique popcorn popper in its candy kitchen. Even better, the viewing windows in the shop are designed to give everyone a front row look at the process, allowing kids and adults to watch the staff confectioners at work. All of these factors contribute to an impressively high Yelp rating, where customers called it cute and charming, with a heavenly smell and friendly staff members.

This candy store won national recognition for its sweet treats, and for decades, has been known for wafting aromas of caramel corn and waffle cones down Walla Walla's Main Street. Try out the chocolates, truffles, and seasonal items like handmade chocolate Easter bunnies. Or, go for fudge, licorice, or colorful frozen treats. In other words, it's not just a candy store; it's a place to immerse all of your senses in sweets. What's not to love about that?

This list was compiled using review sites like Reddit, Google, and Tripadvisor; research on candy stores' websites from coast to coast; and tracking media mentions on major news outlets. Extra attention was given to candy stores that are historic and/or boast unique offerings to visitors, such as mini golf, soda fountains, museums, and more.

#9583. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

Photography by Patrick Marinello; styling by Yekaterina Boytsova

#9580. Forget Plain Butter: Drizzle This Rich Ingredient Over Stuffing For 10x The Flavor

When it comes to the Thanksgiving feast, Americans' favorite sides include mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, and of course, stuffing. Whether it comes from a box or is lovingly homemade, stuffing is a filling, savory, and surprisingly historical part of many Turkey Day spreads. And there are seemingly as many variations of stuffing as there are households in the U.S., but butter is a unifying and necessary ingredient that no version of this Thanksgiving side can go without. However, if you really want to up the richness and flavor of your next casserole dish of stuffing, forget plain old regular butter and instead try brown butter.

Brown butter is most notably used in sweet baked goods, but the golden, nutty version can truly enhance pretty much anything where regular butter is used, including savory dishes like stuffing. What it adds to your T-giving side is a sumptuous, caramelly flavor that creates a world of depth and complexity, as the sweetness of the brown butter beautifully complements all the savory ingredients in the stuffing, like the softened bread cubes, sausage (if you use any), and the fresh herbs.

Don't skimp on it, either. If you're going to use brown butter in stuffing, you'll need to start with quite a bit of butter, perhaps as much as two to three full sticks, because the flavors in your typical stuffing can be bold, and you want to be able to taste the butterscotch-y nuttiness, which pairs so well with sage and onion, or the mushroom in a classic sausage and mushroom stuffing. Even if you make a pumpkin and herb stuffing, full of warming spices and chili, brown butter will enhance the subtle sweetness of the pumpkin and the juiciness of the raisins.

If you're inspired to try using brown butter in your stuffing this year for Thanksgiving, but you've never made it before and you're a little intimidated by it, we've a few tips to get you started. First thing, the color of the pan you use matters because you'll want to keep a close eye on how dark the butter is getting — hard to do in cast iron. The choice is yours whether you use salted or unsalted butter, but you'll want to adjust the seasonings in your stuffing accordingly. It's important that you don't use too high a heat; a good medium to medium-low will do the trick. And finally, don't walk away while your butter is browning because the process is quick, and you can go from delectably golden brown with a nutty aroma to burnt and bitter in a hurry.

There are a number of ways to incorporate brown butter into your stuffing, and whichever you choose, you'll want to remove the pan off the heat as soon as the butter is ready. You might add the veggies, aromatics, and herbs directly into the brown butter pan and let those saturate and saute in the nutty goodness, then add them to the bread element. Or you can remove the brown butter from the pan and keep it aside in a bowl, saute the vegetables, add everything into the waiting bowl of butter, and toss to combine.

#9576. Give Burgers A Protein Boost By Adding One Canned Ingredient To Ground Beef

When you need protein to help support your body after a workout or to keep you satiated throughout the day, you can reach for a number of foods, but we'd venture that there isn't a tastier option than a hamburger or cheeseburger. There are plenty of fast food options that are positively awash in the macronutrient, but cooking at home gives you far more control. Now, ground beef is obviously chock-full of protein, with anywhere from 16 to 24 grams per 4-ounce serving, but if you have a serious goal you need to meet before EOD, there is a canned ingredient that is probably lurking in your pantry (and if it isn't, it should be) that can help push you over the edge. It's beans!

Depending on the type of bean you use, a half-cup typically contains between 7 and 9 grams of protein that you can add to your meat mixture, and ultimately, black beans would be our first choice. Not only are they closest in color to a perfectly grilled burger, but they're surprisingly meaty. When they're mashed and mixed in with the ground beef, they blend right in, and their mild flavor means they take on whatever seasonings you include without drawing attention to themselves (oh, and there's the added bonus that, in addition to the extra protein, they're also a high-fiber food). By the way, if you don't have black beans on hand, you can absolutely use pinto, cannellini, or even red kidney beans.

Canned beans are often packed in a gooey liquid that consists of the starches and other substances that seep out of the beans, mixed with water and sometimes a bit of salt. As such, they are too wet straight out of the can to use in your burger mixture, so you should drain them and then dry them as much as you can (otherwise, your patties could be a soggy mess). You can even help the process by wicking as much moisture out of them as possible, making for a much more desirable texture, by placing them in a single layer on a baking sheet and popping them in the oven for a few minutes.

Mashing the beans by hand before adding them to the ground beef will always be preferable to the evisceration they'd receive in a food processor. Taking a potato masher (or you could use your meat chopper from the Dollar Tree) to the beans produces a variety of different shapes, which is useful not just for aesthetic purposes (the irregularities in the beans mimic the natural lumps that form when burger patties cook), but also for a more satisfyingly hearty bite.

Now, beans and ground beef alone do not a burger patty make; you may want to include some binders to help hold everything together. This might be as simple as an egg or two and breadcrumbs — which type of breadcrumbs is totally up to you, because typical fine-textured crumbs will work, as will panko — plus a condiment of your choice, like ketchup, mustard, or even tangy barbecue sauce.

#9575. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

Cover photo by Mark Weinberg; food styling by Liz Neily.

#9573. For The Best Scrambled Eggs With Extra Fiber, Make Them Turkish Style

Getting your morning fiber doesn't have to be all about eating more fruits or specialty yogurts. Instead, you can deliciously upgrade your scrambled eggs with classic Turkish vegetables in menemen, a sort of low-effort dish that comes loaded with nutrients.

A proper menemen is customizable, but always requires three things: eggs, tomatoes, and peppers. It lets you get so much fiber because it starts with sauteing the vegetables until they soften and reduce in size, so you can load up quite a bit in a single meal. While the exact nutritional profile varies between different types of tomatoes, there's an average of about 2.16 grams of fiber per cup. The sauteing step means you can easily add two cups and cook them down to a thick, jammy consistency, providing a delicious brightness to the eggs just over 4 grams of fiber all in one go.

This is without even mentioning the fiber in the peppers. Banana peppers are relatively high in fiber, clocking in at around 4 grams per cup. Bell peppers are also quite tasty, with some varieties providing about 3 grams per cup. Since the recommended daily fiber intake for most adults hovers between 25 and 38 grams, you could potentially get a substantial portion of your daily needs all in one go. And unlike shakshuka and eggs in purgatory, two similar dishes that traditionally rely on poaching or braising, menemen lets you control the texture quite easily, whether you like your eggs creamy, fluffy, or dense.

Between the rich flavors of menemen and the plethora of foods it can pair with, you've got ample room to deliciously add even more fiber to your breakfast. Taking inspiration from a traditional Turkish breakfast is a great place to start, but don't be afraid to treat your menemen as a starting point rather than a set-in-stone recipe.

Like many countries, Turkey is a big believer in some early morning carbs, and bread products are a great way to add a bit more fiber to your diet. While a slice of white bread may be versatile and provide some sweetness to round out the tomatoes' acidity, one slice also only has about 0.6 grams of fiber. Instead, look to rye, a bread that may not be for everyone but can have three times the fiber of white bread. A slice of pumpernickel can even add 2.7 more grams of fiber to your morning, and the rich, earthy aromas and dense texture are a great contrast to creamy eggs and veggies.

Few fruits are quite so high in fiber as avocado, with a single medium-sized fruit containing around 10 grams of fiber. As a topping for menemen, its rich creaminess works perfectly with the sharper vegetable flavors, while the eggs provide plenty of protein. Half an avocado smeared over pumpernickel and topped with menemen could provide around 16 grams of fiber from all the different sources, roughly half of what many people need per day.

#9571. The Chain Italian Sub With The Best Bread, According To Customer Reviews

Italian sub sandwiches are a thing of beauty: cured meats piled high, creamy cheese, a bit of lettuce and tomato, perhaps a slather of mayo if you're feeling controversial, and maybe a drizzle of herb-infused oil and vinegar. You can find them at pretty much any sandwich shop or deli, though naturally, a number of factors, like size and overall quality, will vary. And while the meats and cheese might be the stars of the show, you cannot discount the importance of good bread. According to a Food Republic roundup of the 10 best chain Italian subs, New York-based chain DiBella's stood out on account of just that, with customers particularly praising its signature everything bread, which adds an extra layer of savory flavor thanks to its topping of seasonings, including ingredients like garlic, poppy seeds, and sesame seeds.

For example, one Reddit user shared that DiBella's version of an Italian, called the Godfather, did not disappoint. "The 'everything' bread was the best part [in my opinion]," they wrote, "but the whole sub was pretty [top-tier] as far as chain restaurants go."

Another reviewer on Yelp also specifically cited the Godfather, saying it was extremely flavorful. "[It] was ridiculously good. So much flavor and taste. The bread really sealed the deal," they praised.

If the glowing reviews have you hankering for a sandwich from a chain you've never heard of before, you're not alone. The reason DiBella's mostly flies under the radar is that it is actually quite limited in locations. As of November 2026, the chain is only present in five states, with the majority of its locations concentrated in New York, its home state, and Ohio. And for the first 80 years of its existence (DiBella's was founded in 1918 as a grocery store), it consisted of just one Rochester location. That changed in 1998, when the company opened its second location, and since then, DiBella's has seen a flurry of expansion, with 2024 proving especially busy.

However, the smaller chain size might actually contribute to the quality of the bread that has put DiBella's on the map, since fewer locations make it easier to maintain standards. For now, in all 44 of the sandwich shop's restaurants, the bread gets baked at least twice daily, as the final step in a process that takes more than half a day. Before the rolls go in the oven, though, the dough gets aged for a minimum of 16 hours to improve texture and taste. Then, seasonings are manually sprinkled on top, and finally, someone wielding a knife hand-scores the tops of the loaves. The frequency of this baking process means that you will almost assuredly get sub rolls at their peak freshness whenever you place your order at DiBella's.

#9568. Olive Garden's Buttery Breadstick Topping Is Actually Dairy-Free

Many diners would agree that one of the biggest pleasures of dining out at Olive Garden isn't just the ambiance or even the appetizers or entrees, like the Tour of Italy, but rather one of the complimentary items that comes with your meal: breadsticks. These soft, pillowy sticks of dough are buttery, garlicky, and great for dipping into dressing or sauces. They are so popular that the chain of Italian-inspired restaurants goes through a staggering number each week, and many diners may even request some extra when taking home leftovers. But despite the buttery flavor of this signature item, it doesn't actually contain any real butter. Instead, the company uses margarine.

Margarine differs from butter in that it is made from oils with a variety of additional ingredients, including water. Together, they form an emulsion that can resemble butter. While not all brands of margarine are completely dairy-free, the kind Olive Garden uses doesn't contain any dairy at all, making it suitable for diners with dairy allergies or those who abstain from animal-derived foods. One reason Olive Garden may use margarine instead of butter is that it can provide a smoother, more consistent topping for its breadsticks.

Butter can also resolidify after it cools, potentially giving the breadsticks a pasty coating. According to Reddit users, Olive Garden uses liquid margarine, which retains its consistency. Additionally, margarine is generally less expensive than butter, and in an industry with razor-thin margins, anywhere you can save money can lead to greater profits.

Perhaps the best use of margarine for Olive Garden fans is to recreate a homemade version of its iconic breadsticks. You can start by using Great Value Garlic Bread Sticks — a fantastic store-bought dupe, available at Walmart — and brushing melted margarine over the sticks after they're heated for an extra buttery finish. Or you can use the melted margarine to give new life to any of the chain's leftover breadsticks you bring home.

Margarine's uses extend well beyond breadsticks, though. For starters, many types of margarine retain a soft texture even when refrigerated, meaning you can easily spread it onto bread or toast even when it's cold. Try doing that with regular butter! Because some types of margarine contain little to no milk solids, they also don't burn as easily as traditional butter does. This means that you can use them to pan-fry foods at relatively higher temperatures than you can with butter without as much risk of altering the flavor of the finished dish.

Finally, margarine is also great for baking. You can often use it in place of butter in the same quantities, though the substitution may affect the finished product. Certain types of margarine also remain solid at higher temperatures, which can be beneficial when baking things like pastries, where fat that melts too quickly can make the difference between beautiful, puffy layers and a flat, greasy end result. Just be sure to avoid spreads or squeezable margarine for baking, as the water content can be too high and negatively affect your recipe.

#9566. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9563. Not Bacon: Give Grilled Cheese A Southern Twist With This Hearty Ingredient

Giving your grilled cheese a Southern twist doesn't mean you have to start using buttermilk biscuits and lard. Instead, you can use ham hocks, a seasoning meat that isn't always actually eaten but is always enjoyable.

The same thing that makes ham hocks delicious also makes them a bit difficult to use. Loaded with bone, connective tissue, and extremely tough meat, bringing out their flavor potential requires a lot of low-and-slow cooking. You may have more luck using smoked ham hocks for a deeper cure and smoke profile, though both smoked and raw hocks still require a long simmer to fully break down the tough collagen before transferring the meat to a sandwich. Regardless, adding shredded ham hock to grilled cheese gives you a tender, protein- and fat-laden ingredient that practically melts right alongside your gooey cheese.

Ham hocks are especially good when you "reuse" them. Cooking one dish with ham hocks and then using the meat in another lets you easily transfer complex flavors, a major tip for making any grilled cheese better. Hocks cooked in Southern-style collard greens adopt a perfectly moist texture and pick up acidity from vinegar and vegetable notes from the greens and onions. Similarly, ones cooked with black-eyed peas have a next-level creaminess, adopting earthy aromas to round out your sandwich. Still, if you want to preserve the smokiness of a fresh smoked ham hock, you can always simmer it for a couple of hours until the meat and skin fall apart, giving you a budget-friendly alternative to pulled pork.

Using ham hocks in your grilled cheese opens up new opportunities, since they're laden with fat and can make excellent use of leaner cheese varieties. Still, you should also consider what part of the hock to use, as some parts have more flavor than others and may require different ratios.

Typically, grilled cheese sandwiches rely on fatty, moisture-rich cheeses because they melt better than drier, aged varieties and carry that rich flavor profile. While you'll still want to use enough for a good texture, ham hocks provide plenty of decadence in their own right, so you can add a heavier sprinkle of Pecorino Romano or Parmigiano Reggiano, aged Gouda, or Manchego viejo. These underrated cheeses can cut through heavier fats more easily and are immediately noticeable even in small quantities, giving you a chance to add more complexity.

When you work with a smoked ham hock, you'll quickly notice how intense the skin's flavor is. Rich in fat and smoky flavor, this is a versatile ingredient you can mash into a spread for your bread, provided it's been properly simmered, or slice thinly and sprinkle in with shredded cheese. The meat directly under the skin is usually pinker and less potent, so it's a great choice if you're looking for more protein but not quite as much smoke. Meat from the top and bottom of the hock may offer a good middle ground, potentially holding more richness and smoke than interior meat but not quite as much as the skin, though this can vary depending on how the hock was smoked and prepared.

#9561. Upgrade Your Next Omelet With One Sweet Pantry Staple

Omelets are one of those dishes that feel made to be upgraded. While meats and vegetables go a long way toward something savory, going in a sweeter direction mixes things up and makes great use of one ingredient you probably already have on hand: honey.

A sweet omelet may sound a bit strange, but it's more common than you might think. Jelly omelets were a hit 100 years ago, and many Japanese folks love atsuyaki tamago, a rolled type of omelet that can be made with sweetened dashi stock. Using honey instead achieves a similar effect but gives you far more control over how your dish turns out. A drizzle over the top while it's still hot warms the honey, helping it spread more evenly and ensuring every bite is as sweet as you want it. Still, you can always mix a dash directly into the eggs, distributing the honey's sweetness throughout the omelet and potentially encouraging a bit of browning as it cooks.

For your first honey omelet, you may want to use something light, like honey made from orange blossom or clover nectar. These aren't overly intense and carry floral notes, and the addition of these aromas can make anyone's mouth water. If you're working with particularly rich eggs, especially duck eggs, you may want to use something with a bit more body, like wildflower or sunflower honey. These have the necessary depth of flavor to stand up to other ingredients and are great when you want a strong honey taste but not too much sweetness.

Honey can be a pretty potent ingredient, so adding too much extra sweetness with reduced tomatoes or caramelized onions can make your dish a bit too decadent in the morning. Instead, try going in the opposite direction, finding ways to add different kinds of saltiness, spice, and astringency for a complex blend of deliciousness.

A swicy flavor profile combines heat from capsaicin and sweetness from honey, both of which balance each other out and go great with eggs. Pork and honey also go together like peas and carrots, so a dollop of chorizo or spiced deli meats in an omelet brings umami, complexity, and harmonious flavors. This is a great opportunity to use hot honey as well, giving you more flexibility with other additions while still getting the same end result. Plus, spicy ingredients can add great color, improving the presentation of your dish to really wow your breakfast guests.

The best cheeses to add are usually sharp, salty, and earthy. Aged parmesan, extra-sharp cheddar, and really anything laden with salt crystals and pungency help balance the sweetness without overshadowing your honey's delicate flavors. Similarly, a bit of raw green onion can taste truly magnificent with honey and egg, but there's an emphasis on "a bit." Too much means you can't taste the honey, so try to aim for a miserly pinch at first and dial in your preference on subsequent attempts.

#9559. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9558. How To Build The Ultimate Aldi Charcuterie Board For Under $25

Everybody loves a charcuterie board, because a charcuterie board has a little something for everybody. But there's a certain art to building a good charcuterie board. A good board is one that offers up an array of different flavors, textures, and colors — each one complimenting the next — all coming together harmoniously to provide the ultimate grazing experience.

Charcuterie boards can add up quickly and can cost a fortune to throw together... but it's perfectly possible to create a great charcuterie board that doesn't break the bank. It all depends where you shop, and one of the best (and most affordable) places you can find your ingredients is at Aldi. In fact, you can build many a beautiful, bountiful board with just $25 thanks to Aldi's highly-rated cheeses, selection of essential cured meats, fresh fruit, crackers, and many more of Aldi's must-have products.

Need some ideas? We've got plenty of ways to build the ultimate charcuterie board that stay within this humble budget to to help make you the host with the most. Note that all of the products and prices below are sourced from an Aldi location in southern California and inventory may vary throughout the country, so be sure to double check your local store's online inventory.

If you want to stick to the tried and true, classic charcuterie board ingredients, you can gather all the hits at Aldi for $25 and build a beautiful board. First (and arguable the most important) stop is the cheese. With Aldi's affordable prices, you can feature three different cheeses which will give the board enough variety — ideally, a classic board combines both soft and hard cheese.

Aldi's private-label brand Emporium Selection has three different cheeses that will not only go together lovely, but will satisfy different tastes and preferences: The Garlic & Herb Gourmet Spreadable Cheese, the Smoked Gouda Cheese, and the Aged Reserved White Cheddar Cheese (it's America's favorite cheese, after all).

Starting with your cheeses, three seasonal picks will be the centerpieces: a Cheddar Parmesan Cheese ($3.95) that will go with all of your other flavors, a 1,000 Day Aged Gouda ($3.99) for that sharp bite, and a Crimson Cranberry White Stilton ($4.19) to really bring it home. Are you cooking up an Italian dinner, or just in the mood for some salty, briny antipasti appetizers? You can create a charcuterie board version of Italian antipasti with several Italian-inspired favorites that you can find at Aldi, and snack like you're in Italy while keeping it all under $25.

For your cheese selection, a fresh log of mozzarella cheese ($3.25) will be the perfect counterpart to the nutty, salty authentic Parmigiano-Reggiano ($6.05) (which is different from Parmesan). If you're feeling a little French, bring some French countryside charm to a rustic charcuterie board using an array of Aldi products that will give your guests a little taste of France. Because who doesn't want that?

Pickled and pickle-flavored foods seem to be all the rage lately, so why not lean in? Turn your party into a pickle party by building a fully pickled-out charcuterie board at Aldi for that punchy hit of briny, vinegary goodness.

#9554. Add This Fresh Herb To Your Bowl Of Chili For 10x The Flavor (Thanks, Ina Garten)

A bowl of chili welcomes a wide array of renditions. You can make the dish red or green, use proteins like turkey, pork, or chicken instead of the classic beef, and include many aromatics in the mix. Each detail makes a chili rendition unique. Even a fresh herb gives a bowl a whole new character — just look toward Ina Garten's inclusion of basil. Ina Garten often uses basil as a swap for cilantro, so her inclusion of the herb in her chili makes sense.

Using the Mediterranean herb in the Tex-Mex recipe may sound unusual, but the flavors align surprisingly well. Garten uses basil's mildly citrusy sweet and lightly peppery flavor specifically in a chicken-based chili, integrating the herb during both the initial simmering stage and as a final garnish. It's a one-two combo that establishes an herbal character that infuses into every bite, lending more than just a basil-inflected finish.

Garten's rendition works the basil into a tomato sauce base, full of sweet bell peppers and onions, lightly recalling a pasta sauce in composition. Still, seasonings like cumin, chili powder, and a dash of spicy cayenne appear in the mix, cementing the dish as a bowl of chili, only brighter and more herbal in nature.

Ina Garten's tips for cooking chicken perfectly dependably deliver, but don't rule out employing the basil in chili recipes with other proteins, too. The herb also works well in an extra-hearty bean and brisket rendition that's spiced with chiles and even coffee. Cooked down right alongside the kidney beans, basil lends the legumes its distinct herbal character, all without becoming a cornerstone flavor. You can try out such a technique in a classic ground beef chili, too; using the herb early in cooking makes it one of many layered flavors.

If you're after a more basil-forward spin, consider working the herb into a ground turkey chili recipe. You can still go heavy on the spice, using chili powder and jalapeños alongside garlic powder and cumin. Add dried basil early on and raw basil atop the finished chili, and you'll get a delicate bowl, herbal-tasting and fresh, yet still pretty classic.

And for a more inventive approach, take a page from Thai cuisine, specifically Phat ka-phrao (stir-fried basil beef). Made with sturdier Thai basil, this version of the herb stands up better to heat. Saute the meat alongside extra-spicy chiles, lots of garlic, and this type of basil, and you can lay down the foundation for an extra-bold chili, still delicious over rice or with tortilla chips.

#9553. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9550. Upgrade Tuna Salad With A Boxed Ingredient That Improves Texture

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Tuna salad is a pragmatic yet delicious dish, easily crafted using pantry staples. Open up some canned fish packed in oil or water, mix with store-bought mayo, then fold in some aromatics, and you'll have yourself a tasty classic. It's a tried-and-true formula that welcomes many other shelf-stable components, like panko bread crumbs, for example. You only need about 2 tablespoons per can of tuna to round things out nicely.

The delicate breadcrumb style is wonderfully versatile in the kitchen, and its texture enhances tuna salad, too. The foodstuff lends the dish more body, without turning it too dense. The panko absorbs moisture, making the crumbs turn soft while still retaining airiness, in turn creating an extra-tender salad. The panko also thickens the dish, giving your meal more structure. Not to mention, a bite here or there might still remain crunchy, upping the textural intrigue.

It's an advantageous set of qualities unique specifically to panko; you won't want to reach for a different breadcrumb in this application, as they may be too dense. This Japanese foodstuff is made using a unique electric cooking process, producing a delicate crumble without any bread crust. Other breadcrumb varieties are simply too heavy for the task. So grab a package of panko online or in stores to make a tuna salad rendition with a textural twist.

Not sure how to round out a tuna salad with panko? The options are wide-ranging. You could keep to a straightforward mix of tuna, mayo, salt, and pepper — perfect for a tuna sandwich filling — or go with the many potential tuna salad upgrades. Walnuts or kimchi, for example, add body and even more texture to the dish.

Similarly, to complement panko's delicate composition, throw in some vegetables. Green onion, celery, and an herb, say parsley, dill, or cilantro, are tried-and-true tuna salad enhancements. And don't overlook a tangy fermented bite, whether in the form of pickles or pickled onions for a truly amped up tuna salad. You could also imbue brightness using vinegar or even lime juice, which will aromatically soak into the panko.

Alternatively, consider playing to the breadcrumb's East Asian origins, using other Japanese ingredients in the dish. You could add a couple spoonfuls of miso into the dressing for complex savory flavors, as well as sesame seeds and oil for a discernible nutty touch. Or go down the spicy tuna route, incorporating a hot sauce like Sriracha into the build — especially tasty when wrapped in seaweed. Swap the standard mayo for a Japanese-style emulsion, mix in the panko, and you'll have yourself a magical tuna salad foundation.

#9549. Scrambled Eggs Get A Major Protein And Flavor Boost When You Add This Omega-Rich Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When many of us think "hot breakfast," we tend to naturally gravitate toward thoughts of scrambled eggs. Aside from the fact that, when prepared correctly, they are tender, delicate, and fluffy (or custardy, depending on how you like them), eggs are considered the gold standard for protein, so they are quite wholesome as well. On their own, though, they can get a little monotonous, especially if you're making them every day, so it does help to add an ingredient here or there. And if you happen to enjoy omega-3-rich cold-smoked salmon, well, it pairs seamlessly with a classic scramble, boosting both the flavor and the protein content.

Once considered an expensive delicacy, smoked salmon is quite popular now in the U.S., and as a result, it's much easier to find at your local grocery store (even Aldi carries its own version, and it can be found at Walmart, too). Cold-smoked salmon, despite the fact that it tends to be packed in super-thin slices, is buttery and velvety. While it does taste fishy, there are also light, smoky notes that give it a deeply savory flavor, which works beautifully when combined with the mild egg scramble. Additionally, a serving (which will vary in size) might contain anywhere from 12 to 18 grams of protein, which is great if you have daily goals you want to meet or you're just looking to get more of the macronutrient in general.

Truly, the most difficult part about incorporating smoked salmon into your scramble is cooking the eggs to the right consistency without burning or browning them. All you have to do with the salmon is slice the ultra-thin pieces into slivers or small squares. Once your eggs have reached the texture you desire, you'll take the pan off the heat and fold in the salmon. That's literally it; you don't have to actually cook the salmon over direct heat because it's so delicate that the residual warmth of the scrambled eggs will gently bring it up to temperature.

Now, because smoked salmon is so light and thin, you might want your eggs to match that energy, so create a fluffy, soft texture with a bit of cream whisked in. Alternatively, you could take a page out of Bobby Flay's book and fold in a dollop of crème fraîche, or really up the decadence and melt in some cubes of cream cheese (and take care not to overcook anything, because smoked salmon with burnt, rubbery eggs? No thanks). Also, because all of the elements involved are either rich or thick, a sprinkling of something green, like fresh chives or dill, or even a little parsley or tarragon, would brighten things up, both aesthetically and in terms of flavor.

#9547. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

#9546. Forget Expensive Ribeye: A Cheaper Cut For Delicious Beef Stroganoff

Indulgently and immensely comforting, beef stroganoff is one of those low-effort meals you make when you just want to feel good. But one thing that might not lift your spirits is the price. Classic stroganoff starts off with strips of thinly sliced beef, with cuts like ribeye being among the best picks. We're not here to fault ribeye, which has earned its price for a reason, but if you want to knock a few dollars off your next batch, try swapping in ground beef instead.

While it may not satisfy the purist, and might even horrify a Russian (the dish's country of origin), we'd argue that ground beef is a worthy alternative to any traditional whole cut of steak. The texture is bound to be different, and you'll need to adjust how you cook it, but good-quality ground beef still has the rich, beefy flavor that pairs so well with the tang of sour cream, earthy mushrooms, and the sweet depth of cooked-down onions, all at a significantly lower cost.

Another reason ground beef works so well here is its cooking time. Traditional beef stroganoff relies on expensive cuts that are prized for their tenderness and quick-cooking nature. Cheaper, tougher cuts like chuck or round usually need hours of braising to soften, which doesn't suit a dish that's meant to come together quickly. Ground beef, however, is often made from those same economical cuts, and the grinding process does all the tenderizing mechanically. That means you're getting all that mouthwatering flavor without the waiting, guaranteeing a tasty, Boomer-approved meal.

If you make the switch from ribeye to ground beef, you'll want to do a few things differently. First, check out the numbers on your ground beef packaging. You're looking for a blend that doesn't shy away from fat, something like an 80-to-20 lean-to-fat ratio, or even 70-to-30. Like ribeye, these fattier blends are packed with rich flavor, and the fat that'll render out will elevate the sauce, just in a different format. Go any leaner and you risk dry, chewy beef pebbles floating in your sauce.

With ribeye, standard practice is to slice the beef ultra-thin, give it a quick sear, then let it simmer in the sauce for a few minutes. The process for ground beef is similar, albeit with a few caveats. For starters, there's no slicing, so you're already saving time. Like ribeye, you want to get the meat nicely browned. Our personal advice is to add the beef to the pan in small handfuls and flatten each one with the back of a spoon, which allows it to brown without overcrowding the pan.

Remove the beef from the pan once it's seared, which isn't usually done with ribeye. Even in a fattier blend, ground beef has far more exposed surface area than your average slice of steak, so it risks drying out if it's left to simmer for too long. For the most tender results, build your sauce first, then add the beef back in and stir once you're just about ready to serve. Don't worry about the flavors not melding, since the fat and fond left behind from searing will be doing most of the heavy lifting.

#9545. This Chain Serves The Best Old-School Italian Sub, According To Customer Reviews

You might not expect it, but sandwich chains are holding it down when it comes to Italian subs. Of course, there is no denying the appeal of a small, locally owned shop, but there are many reasons why you might opt instead to head into a chain to get your Italian hoagie fix, the most obvious of which is proximity. But there is also the fact that some chains just make darn good food. Food Republic did its research and compiled a list of the best chain Italian subs based on customer reviews, and each entry brings its own unique flavor to the table. But only one, the No. 13 Original Italian from Jersey Mike's, can claim to be the best old-school version of this particular sub.

"They do it right," one Reddit user said, referencing the Original Italian. They continued by stating that if they had a classic Italian deli near them, they'd go there, but since they don't, "it's Jersey Mike's without question." Another user in that same thread agreed, writing, "I love this sub and am always a little amazed [it comes from] a chain" and not, presumably, from a traditional deli. And over on Google, a reviewer shared that the Original Italian reminded them of a sub they'd had during their childhood and expressed their gratitude that "there is a place that can make a real Italian hero like the old days."

It's worth noting that an old-school-style Italian sub owes it all to the Italian immigrants who populated this country throughout the 19th and 20th centuries. There are a few stories about how the hoagie came to be, including one based in Philadelphia (where it's the official sandwich of the city) involving shipyard workers and their distinctive lunches. There is another version that describes how Giovanna Amato sold filling sandwiches to dockworkers in Maine. Whatever its origins, the classic Italian sub came to be characterized by Italian meats and cheeses, a variety of fresh, crisp vegetables, a savory dressing, and an oily, vinegary drizzle.

Jersey Mike's Original Italian proves a chain can still honor those old-school roots. It checks every box, from five different Italian meats to provolone cheese to the default setting, Mike's Way, which includes onions, lettuce sliced super-thin, and tomatoes, as well as red wine vinegar and an olive oil blend, plus two impactful seasonings: salt and oregano.

But of course, Jersey Mike's serves 21st-century customers who like having options, so the sandwich, in addition to scratching an old-school itch, can also serve as a jumping-off point for some. You might, for example, upgrade your Original Italian sub by choosing the rosemary parmesan bread instead of plain white.
